    ny, nx = 8, 12; jj, ii = np.mgrid[:ny, :nx].astype(float); f = 3*jj + 2*ii + 1; w = 1 + (jj+ii) % 3
    for name, fn in (("T2UV", grid_c.interp_T2UV), ("1D", grid_c.interp_1D)):
        ok(f"{name} lon linear", rerr(fn(f, orca.halo, dir="lon")[:, :-1], (f + 1.0)[:, :-1]), 1e-14)
        ok(f"{name} lat linear", rerr(fn(f, orca.halo, dir="lat")[:-1], (f + 1.5)[:-1]), 1e-14)
        ok(f"{name} lon weighted, constant stays", rerr(fn(0*f+7, orca.halo, weights_in=w, dir="lon"), 7.), 1e-14)
        h = (w[:, :-1]*f[:, :-1] + w[:, 1:]*f[:, 1:])/(w[:, :-1]+w[:, 1:])
        ok(f"{name} lon weighted, hand value", rerr(fn(f, orca.halo, weights_in=w, dir="lon")[:, :-1], h), 1e-14)
        h = (w[:-1]*f[:-1] + w[1:]*f[1:])/(w[:-1]+w[1:])
        ok(f"{name} lat weighted, hand value", rerr(fn(f, orca.halo, weights_in=w, dir="lat")[:-1], h), 1e-14)
    ok("UV2T lon linear", rerr(grid_c.interp_UV2T(f, orca.halo, dir="lon")[:, 1:], (f - 1.0)[:, 1:]), 1e-14)
    ok("UV2T lat linear", rerr(grid_c.interp_UV2T(f, orca.halo, dir="lat")[1:], (f - 1.5)[1:]), 1e-14)
    ok("UV2T lon weighted, constant", rerr(grid_c.interp_UV2T(0*f+7, orca.halo, weights_in=w, dir="lon"), 7.), 1e-14)
    ok("UV2T lat weighted, constant", rerr(grid_c.interp_UV2T(0*f+7, orca.halo, weights_in=w, dir="lat"), 7.), 1e-14)

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › fdiff_1D

fdiff_1D

Forward difference along x or along y, divided by a scale factor.

Description

Gradients on the C grid are differences between neighbours divided by the distance between them, and they land half a cell forward: the x-gradient of a T-point field sits on U-points. The weights are that distance, e.g. e1u for d/dx of a T field.

The neighbour after the last column or row comes from the halo, with the fold rule of `point`.

$$(\delta_i f)_{i,j} = \frac{f_{i+1,j} - f_{i,j}}{e_{i,j}},\qquad (\delta_j f)_{i,j} = \frac{f_{i,j+1} - f_{i,j}}{e_{i,j}}$$

Syntax

field_out = fdiff_1D(field_in, weights_in, exchange)field_out = fdiff_1D(field_in, weights_in, exchange, dir=None, isMeridional=False, point='T')

Input Arguments

field_in — float
Field to be differentiated
weights_in — float
Metric (e.g. e1/e2 scale factor)
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, see module docstring
dir — str — default None
Direction of differentiation, 'lon' or 'lat'
isMeridional — bool — default False
if True, change the sign of the north halo
point — str — default 'T'
Where field_in lives, 'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F'

Output Arguments

field_out — float
Resulting field

Example

dx = grid_c.fdiff_1D(psi, g["e1u"], orca.halo, dir="lon")
dy = grid_c.fdiff_1D(psi, g["e2v"], orca.halo, dir="lat")
Whole test
with test("orcakit.grid_c.fdiff_1D", "orcakit.grid_c.bdiff_1D"):
    g = sph(360, 180); DL = 2*np.pi/358; DP = 2*(np.pi/3)/180; p, l = g["lat_t"], g["lon_t"]; psi = np.cos(p)*np.cos(2*l)
    dx = grid_c.fdiff_1D(psi, g["e1u"], orca.halo, dir="lon")
    ok("fdiff lon at U-points", rerr(dx[1:-1], (-2*np.sin(2*g["lon_u"])/A)[1:-1]), 2e-3)
    dy = grid_c.fdiff_1D(psi, g["e2v"], orca.halo, dir="lat")
    ok("fdiff lat at V-points", rerr(dy[1:-2], (-np.sin(g["lat_v"])*np.cos(2*l)/A)[1:-2]), 2e-3)
    bx = grid_c.bdiff_1D(psi, g["e1u"], orca.halo, dir="lon")
    ok("bdiff lon at U(i-1/2)", rerr(bx[1:-1], (-2*np.sin(2*(l-DL/2))/A)[1:-1]), 2e-3)
    by = grid_c.bdiff_1D(psi, g["e2t"], orca.halo, dir="lat")
    ok("bdiff lat at V(j-1/2)", rerr(by[1:-1], (-np.sin(p-DP/2)*np.cos(2*l)/A)[1:-1]), 3e-3)
    z = grid_c.vort_Vgrid(dx, dy, g["e1v"], g["e2t"], g["e1u"], g["e2v"], orca.halo)
    ok("curl grad = 0, relative to |grad|/dx", np.abs(z[1:-2]).max()/(np.abs(dy).max()/g["e2t"].max()), 1e-12)
    pf = np.cos(g["lat_v"])*np.cos(2*g["lon_u"])
    uu = -grid_c.bdiff_1D(pf, g["e2u"], orca.halo, dir="lat"); vv = grid_c.bdiff_1D(pf, g["e1v"], orca.halo, dir="lon")
    d = grid_c.hDiv_Vgrid(uu, vv, g["e1t"], g["e2t"], g["e1v"], g["e2u"], orca.halo)
    ok("div curl = 0, relative to |u|/dx", np.abs(d[2:-2]).max()/(np.abs(uu).max()/g["e2t"].max()), 1e-12)

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › bdiff_1D

bdiff_1D

Backward difference along x or along y, divided by a scale factor.

Description

The backward counterpart of fdiff_1D, for gradients that land half a cell back, for example from U-points to T-points along x.

Along x the neighbour before column 0 comes from the periodic seam. Along y row 0 has no neighbour below and is set to 0; on the ORCA grids that row is land.

$$(\delta_i f)_{i,j} = \frac{f_{i,j} - f_{i-1,j}}{e_{i,j}},\qquad (\delta_j f)_{i,j} = \frac{f_{i,j} - f_{i,j-1}}{e_{i,j}}$$

Syntax

field_out = bdiff_1D(field_in, weights_in, exchange)field_out = bdiff_1D(field_in, weights_in, exchange, dir=None, isMeridional=False)

Input Arguments

field_in — float
Field to be differentiated
weights_in — float
Metric (e.g. e1/e2 scale factor)
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, see module docstring
dir — str — default None
Direction of differentiation, 'lon' or 'lat'
isMeridional — bool — default False
if True, change the sign of the north halo

Output Arguments

field_out — float
Resulting field

Example

bx = grid_c.bdiff_1D(psi, g["e1u"], orca.halo, dir="lon")
by = grid_c.bdiff_1D(psi, g["e2t"], orca.halo, dir="lat")
uu = -grid_c.bdiff_1D(pf, g["e2u"], orca.halo, dir="lat"); vv = grid_c.bdiff_1D(pf, g["e1v"], orca.halo, dir="lon")

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › dxFu_1D

dxFu_1D

The zonal part of a flux divergence on T-points.

Description

A divergence on the C grid is the difference of the fluxes through the faces of a cell. This is the x part alone: the flux e2u u through each east face, differenced with the west face and divided by e1t.

The west face of column 0 comes from the periodic seam.

$$\frac{(e_{2u}\,u)_{i,j} - (e_{2u}\,u)_{i-1,j}}{e_{1t}}$$

Syntax

field_out = dxFu_1D(u, e1t, e2u, exchange)

Input Arguments

u — float
Zonal, X-directed velocity (U-point)
e1t — float
Metric term on T-point (output grid)
e2u — float
Metric term on U-point (building the flux)
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, see module docstring

Output Arguments

field_out — float
d(Fu)/dx, on T-points Note: the parameter names used to be swapped (e1u, e2t) and Fu was built as u*e2t -- a T-point metric applied to a U-point velocity with no interpolation. Also used an east-halo/forward-difference, which is the wrong direction for a T-point divergence (needs the backward neighbour, see hDiv_Vgrid). Both fixed here, matching hDiv_Vgrid's (verified) Dlon_Fu convention.

Example

d = grid_c.dxFu_1D(u, g["e1t"], g["e2u"], orca.halo)
Whole test
with test("orcakit.grid_c.dxFu_1D"):
    g = sph(360, 180); u = np.cos(g["lat_t"])*np.sin(2*g["lon_u"])
    d = grid_c.dxFu_1D(u, g["e1t"], g["e2u"], orca.halo)
    ok("against 2 e2u cos(2 lambda)/a", rerr(d, 2*g["e2u"]*np.cos(2*g["lon_t"])/A), 2e-3)

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › hDiv_Vgrid

hDiv_Vgrid

Horizontal divergence on T-points of velocities on U-points and V-points.

Description

The divergence measures how much flow leaves a cell: the net flux through its four faces, each the velocity times the face width, divided by the cell area. It is the C-grid form NEMO uses, and with transports e3u u and e3v v in place of u and v it gives the transport divergence that sets the vertical velocity.

The west face of column 0 comes from the periodic seam. Row 0 has no south face and gets no meridional term; on the ORCA grids that row is land.

$$\nabla_h\cdot\mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{e_{1t}e_{2t}}\Big[(e_{2u}u)_{i,j} - (e_{2u}u)_{i-1,j} + (e_{1v}v)_{i,j} - (e_{1v}v)_{i,j-1}\Big]$$

Syntax

field_out = hDiv_Vgrid(u, v, dx_t, dy_t, dx_v, dy_u, exchange)field_out = hDiv_Vgrid(u, v, dx_t, dy_t, dx_v, dy_u, exchange, isMeridional=False)

Input Arguments

u — float
Zonal, X-directed velocity
v — float
Meridional, Y-directed velocity
dx_t,dy_t — float
Metric terms on T-point
dx_v — float
Metric terms on V-point
dy_u — float
Metric terms on U-point
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, see module docstring
isMeridional — bool — default False
if True, change the sign of the north halo

Output Arguments

field_out — float
Resulting field Usage: divH = hDiv_Vgrid(u, v, e1t, e2t, e1v, e2u, orca.halo)

Example

d = grid_c.hDiv_Vgrid(u, v, g["e1t"], g["e2t"], g["e1v"], g["e2u"], orca.halo)
d = grid_c.hDiv_Vgrid(u, v, g["e1t"], g["e2t"], g["e1v"], g["e2u"], orca.halo)
Whole test
with test("orcakit.grid_c.hDiv_Vgrid"):

    ok("discrete divergence theorem, sum/(sum|.|)", np.sum((d*g["e1t"]*g["e2t"])[:, 1:-1])/np.sum(np.abs(d*g["e1t"]*g["e2t"])[:, 1:-1]), 1e-13)

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › w_from_divergence

w_from_divergence

Vertical velocity by integrating the divergence up from the bottom.

Description

Incompressible flow that converges in a layer must leave it vertically. Starting from w = 0 below the deepest level, each level adds the divergence times its thickness, which gives w at the top of every T-cell, as NEMO computes it.

Levels are axis -3, surface first. The divergence is counted only on wet points.

$$w_k = w_{k+1} - e_{3t,k}\,(\nabla_h\cdot\mathbf{u})_k\,t_k,\qquad w = 0 \text{ below the deepest level}$$

Syntax

w = w_from_divergence(div, e3t, tmask)

Input Arguments

div — float
(..., nz, ny, nx) horizontal divergence at T-points, in s-1
e3t — float
(..., nz, ny, nx) T-cell thicknesses, in metres, or broadcastable
tmask — float
(..., nz, ny, nx) T-point wet mask

Output Arguments

w — float
(..., nz, ny, nx) vertical velocity at the top of T-cells, in m/s

Example

dl = 2e-6; e3 = 10*np.ones((5, 2, 2)); tm = np.ones((5, 2, 2)); tm[-1] = 0; w = grid_c.w_from_divergence(dl*tm, e3, tm)
Whole test

    ok("w_k = -delta e3 (4-k)", w[:, 0, 0] + dl*10*(4-np.arange(5)), 1e-18)
    ok("the real meshes have a dry last level, which this relies on", [glorys04.mesh("tmask")[-1].sum(), cmems.mesh("tmask")[-1].sum()], 0)

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › vertical_velocity

vertical_velocity

Vertical velocity from horizontal velocity, by continuity, as NEMO computes it.

Description

Many products store u and v but not w, though w follows from them: what converges horizontally in a layer must leave it vertically. Here the fluxes through each face carry the face's thickness, so the partial cells at the sea floor are counted with their true size and no T-cell thickness is needed. On a NEMO grid this reproduces the model's own w.

w sits at the top of each T-cell, zero below the deepest level. Velocities on land count as 0, and the result is NaN on land.

$$w_k = w_{k+1} - \frac{(e_{2u}e_{3u}u)_{i,j} - (e_{2u}e_{3u}u)_{i-1,j} + (e_{1v}e_{3v}v)_{i,j} - (e_{1v}e_{3v}v)_{i,j-1}}{e_{1t}e_{2t}}\bigg|_k,\qquad w = 0 \text{ at the bottom}$$

Syntax

w = vertical_velocity(u, v, e1t, e2t, e1v, e2u, e3u, e3v, umask, vmask, tmask, exchange)

Input Arguments

u — float
(nz, ny, nx) U-point velocity, may hold NaN on land
v — float
(nz, ny, nx) V-point velocity, may hold NaN on land
e1t — float
(ny, nx) T-cell widths along x, in metres
e2t — float
(ny, nx) T-cell widths along y, in metres
e1v — float
(ny, nx) V-cell widths along x, in metres
e2u — float
(ny, nx) U-cell widths along y, in metres
e3u — float
(nz, ny, nx) U-cell thicknesses, in metres
e3v — float
(nz, ny, nx) V-cell thicknesses, in metres
umask — array
(nz, ny, nx) U-point wet mask
vmask — array
(nz, ny, nx) V-point wet mask
tmask — array
(nz, ny, nx) T-point wet mask
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, e.g. orca.halo

Output Arguments

w — float
(nz, ny, nx) vertical velocity at the top of T-cells, in m/s; NaN on land

Example

WV = lambda a, b, m: grid_c.vertical_velocity(a, b, exchange=orca.halo, **m)
Whole test
with test(*[f"datakit._source.Source.{m}" for m in ("__init__", "files", "read", "stream", "groups", "mesh", "grid", "vertical", "coords", "depth", "time_hours", "snapshot")], "datakit._source.source", "datakit._source.derived", "datakit._write.write_field", "datakit._write.provenance", "datakit._write.history", "preprocessing.baroclinic.split", "orcakit.grid_c.vertical_velocity", "datakit._source.Source.point_mask", "datakit._source.Source.point_coords", "orcakit.paths.get"):
    from orcakit import paths as PA
    toml = os.path.join(TMP, "paths.toml")
    with open(toml, "w") as t_: t_.write('one = "~/x"\n')
    saved = os.environ.get("LU_PATHS"); os.environ["LU_PATHS"] = toml
    yes("location read, with ~ expanded", PA.get("one") == os.path.expanduser("~/x"))
    yes("unset location gives a placeholder that names it", "two" in PA.get("two") and "not set" in PA.get("two"))
    if saved is None: del os.environ["LU_PATHS"]
    else: os.environ["LU_PATHS"] = saved
    nz, ny, nx = 3, 12, 16; e3 = np.array([10., 20., 30.]); mesh = os.path.join(TMP, "stage0_mesh.nc")
    tm = np.ones((nz, ny, nx), "i1"); tm[:, 5, 6] = 0
    um = tm*np.roll(tm, -1, axis=2); vm = tm*np.roll(tm, -1, axis=1)
    with netCDF4.Dataset(mesh, "w") as nc:
        for d, s in (("t", 1), ("z", nz), ("y", ny), ("x", nx)): nc.createDimension(d, s)
        nc.createVariable("e3t_0", "f8", ("t", "z"))[:] = e3
        nc.createVariable("e3t_ps", "f8", ("t", "y", "x"))[:] = e3[-1]
        for n_, a in (("tmask", tm), ("umask", um), ("vmask", vm)): nc.createVariable(n_, "i1", ("t", "z", "y", "x"))[:] = a
        for n_ in ("gphit", "glamt", "gphiu", "glamu", "e1t", "e2t", "e1u", "e2u", "e1v", "e2v", "e1f", "e2f"): nc.createVariable(n_, "f8", ("t", "y", "x"))[:] = 1000.
    S = SRC.Source("fake", os.path.join(TMP, "stage0_raw"), [mesh], "fk", 86400.)
    e3u, e3v, u_m, v_m = S.vertical(np.float64)
    yes("masks returned as boolean", u_m.dtype == bool and v_m.dtype == bool)
    ok("e3u is e3t_0 on wet points", (e3u - e3[:, None, None])[:, 1:-2, 1:-2][u_m[:, 1:-2, 1:-2]], 1e-12)

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › geostrophic_uv

geostrophic_uv

Surface geostrophic velocity from sea surface height.

Description

Away from the equator and the coasts, the large-scale surface flow is close to geostrophic balance: it follows the lines of constant sea level, faster where they are closer. This gives that flow on the full grid, so it can be compared with the model's velocity or used where only sea level is known.

SSH is averaged to F-points over wet T-points only, then differenced onto U-points and V-points, with the Coriolis parameter at each of them. Within about 5 degrees of the equator geostrophy does not hold and the result is NaN; within about two cells of land the wet-only average biases it.

$$\eta_f = \frac{\sum_{4\,T} A\,\eta}{\sum_{4\,T} A}\ \text{(wet T-points only)},\qquad A = e_{1t}e_{2t}$$
$$U_g = -\frac{g}{f_u}\,\frac{\eta_f(i,j) - \eta_f(i,j-1)}{e_{2u}},\qquad V_g = \frac{g}{f_v}\,\frac{\eta_f(i,j) - \eta_f(i-1,j)}{e_{1v}},\qquad f = 2\Omega\sin\varphi$$

Syntax

Ug, Vg = geostrophic_uv(ssh, tmask, umask, vmask, e1t, e2t, e1v, e2u, gphiu, gphiv, exchange)Ug, Vg = geostrophic_uv(ssh, tmask, umask, vmask, e1t, e2t, e1v, e2u, gphiu, gphiv, exchange, min_lat=5.0, gravity=9.80665, omega=7.292116e-05)

Input Arguments

ssh — float
(ny, nx) sea surface height, in metres; NaN counts as land
tmask — bool
(ny, nx) T-point wet mask
umask — bool
(ny, nx) U-point wet mask
vmask — bool
(ny, nx) V-point wet mask
e1t — float
(ny, nx) T-cell widths along x, in metres
e2t — float
(ny, nx) T-cell widths along y, in metres
e1v — float
(ny, nx) V-cell widths along x, in metres
e2u — float
(ny, nx) U-cell widths along y, in metres
gphiu — float
(ny, nx) latitude of U-points, in degrees
gphiv — float
(ny, nx) latitude of V-points, in degrees
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, e.g. orca.halo
min_lat — float — default 5.0
Latitude, in degrees, below which the result is NaN
gravity — float — default 9.80665
Gravity, in m s-2; NEMO's value by default
omega — float — default 7.292116e-05
Earth's rotation rate, in s-1

Output Arguments

Ug — float
(ny, nx) zonal velocity on U-points, in m/s; NaN on land, for |lat| < min_lat and on row 0
Vg — float
(ny, nx) meridional velocity on V-points, in m/s; NaN on land and for |lat| < min_lat

Example

Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(al*jj*dy, W, exchange=orca.halo, **kw)
Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(be*ii*dx, W, exchange=orca.halo, **kw)
Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(al*jj*dy, W, exchange=orca.halo, **{**kw, "gphiu": 2.*O, "gphiv": 2.*O}); yes("NaN below min_lat", np.isnan(Ug).all() and np.isnan(Vg).all())
Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(s_, Ld, exchange=orca.halo, **{**kw, "umask": um_, "vmask": vm_}); yes("land does not spread NaN to wet points", np.isfinite(Ug[10:20, 10:30][um_[10:20, 10:30]]).all())
Whole test
with test("orcakit.grid_c.geostrophic_uv"):
    dx, dy, f0, al, be = 1e4, 2e4, 1e-4, 1e-6, 2e-6; ny_, nx_ = 30, 40; O = np.ones((ny_, nx_)); lat0 = np.degrees(np.arcsin(f0/(2*7.292116e-5)))
    jj, ii = np.mgrid[:ny_, :nx_]; W = O.astype(bool); kw = dict(umask=W, vmask=W, e1t=dx*O, e2t=dy*O, e1v=dx*O, e2u=dy*O, gphiu=lat0*O, gphiv=lat0*O)
    Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(al*jj*dy, W, exchange=orca.halo, **kw)
    ok("Ug from a northward slope", Ug[2:-5, 2:-3] + 9.80665*al/f0, 1e-9); ok("no Vg from it", Vg[2:-5, 2:-3], 1e-9)
    Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(be*ii*dx, W, exchange=orca.halo, **kw)
    ok("Vg from an eastward slope", Vg[2:-5, 2:-3] - 9.80665*be/f0, 1e-9); ok("no Ug from it", Ug[2:-5, 2:-3], 1e-9)
    yes("row 0 of Ug is NaN", np.isnan(Ug[0]).all())
    Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(al*jj*dy, W, exchange=orca.halo, **{**kw, "gphiu": 2.*O, "gphiv": 2.*O}); yes("NaN below min_lat", np.isnan(Ug).all() and np.isnan(Vg).all())
    Ld = W.copy(); Ld[15, 20] = False; s_ = al*jj*dy; s_ = np.where(Ld, s_, np.nan); um_ = Ld & np.roll(Ld, -1, 1); vm_ = Ld & np.roll(Ld, -1, 0)
    Ug, Vg = grid_c.geostrophic_uv(s_, Ld, exchange=orca.halo, **{**kw, "umask": um_, "vmask": vm_}); yes("land does not spread NaN to wet points", np.isfinite(Ug[10:20, 10:30][um_[10:20, 10:30]]).all())
    yes("land is NaN", np.isnan(Ug[15, 20]) and np.isnan(Ug[15, 19]) and np.isnan(Vg[15, 20]))

geostrophic_uv.corner_sum

Sum of each 2 x 2 block, the four T-points around an F-point.

Description

A helper of geostrophic_uv, for the area-weighted average of SSH onto F-points.

$$s_{j,i} = a_{j,i} + a_{j+1,i} + a_{j+1,i+1} + a_{j,i+1}$$

Syntax

s = corner_sum(a)

Input Arguments

a — float
(ny+1, nx+2) padded array

Output Arguments

s — float
(ny, nx+1) sums

Example

No test of its own; see the routines that call it.

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › hDiv_Tgrid

hDiv_Tgrid

Horizontal divergence on T-points of velocities that are themselves on T-points.

Description

For velocities already averaged or interpolated to the cell centres, as some datasets store them. They are first averaged onto the faces, then their fluxes are differenced as in hDiv_Vgrid.

The halo supplies the neighbours beyond the last column and row, with the sign flip at the fold for v. Row 0 gets no meridional term.

$$\nabla_h\cdot\mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{e_{1t}e_{2t}}\Big[(e_{2u}\overline{u}^{\,i})_{i,j} - (e_{2u}\overline{u}^{\,i})_{i-1,j} + (e_{1v}\overline{v}^{\,j})_{i,j} - (e_{1v}\overline{v}^{\,j})_{i,j-1}\Big]$$

Syntax

field_out = hDiv_Tgrid(u, v, e1t, e2t, e1v, e2u, exchange)field_out = hDiv_Tgrid(u, v, e1t, e2t, e1v, e2u, exchange, isMeridional=True)

Input Arguments

u — float
Zonal, X-directed velocity
v — float
Meridional, Y-directed velocity
e1t, e2t — float
Metric terms on T-point
e1v — float
Metric terms on V-point
e2u — float
Metric terms on U-point
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, see module docstring
isMeridional — bool — default True
if True, change the sign of v's north halo

Output Arguments

field_out — float
Resulting field. Row 0 has no meridional term. Usage: divH = hDiv_Tgrid(u, v, e1t, e2t, e1v, e2u, orca.halo)

Example

d = grid_c.hDiv_Tgrid(u, v, g["e1t"], g["e2t"], g["e1v"], g["e2u"], orca.halo)
Whole test
with test("orcakit.grid_c.hDiv_Tgrid"):
    E = []
    for N in (180, 360):
        g = sph(N, N//2); p, l = g["lat_t"], g["lon_t"]
        u, v = np.cos(p)*np.sin(2*l), np.cos(p)*np.sin(p)*np.cos(3*l)
        d = grid_c.hDiv_Tgrid(u, v, g["e1t"], g["e2t"], g["e1v"], g["e2u"], orca.halo)
        E.append(np.max(np.abs(d - div_exact(g))[1:-1, 1:]))
    ok("relative error, N=360, excluding column 0", E[1]/np.abs(div_exact(g)).max(), 2e-3)
    ok("order of accuracy minus 2", np.log2(E[0]/E[1]) - 2, 0.2)
    ok("relative error on column 0", np.max(np.abs(d - div_exact(g))[1:-1, 0])/np.abs(div_exact(g)).max(), 2e-3)

py-kits › orcakit › grid_c › vort_Vgrid

vort_Vgrid

Relative vorticity on F-points of velocities on U-points and V-points.

Description

Vorticity measures the local rotation of the flow, positive for anticlockwise rotation seen from above. On the C grid it sits at the corners of the cells, from the circulation of u and v around each corner divided by its area, as in NEMO's vorticity term.

The neighbours beyond the last column and row come from the halo, with the sign flip of both velocity components at the fold.

$$\zeta_{i,j} = \frac{1}{e_{1f}e_{2f}}\Big[(e_{2v}v)_{i+1,j} - (e_{2v}v)_{i,j} - (e_{1u}u)_{i,j+1} + (e_{1u}u)_{i,j}\Big]$$

Syntax

field_out = vort_Vgrid(u, v, dx_f, dy_f, dx_u, dy_v, exchange)

Input Arguments

u — float
Zonal, X-directed velocity
v — float
Meridional, Y-directed velocity
dx_f,dy_f — float
Metric terms on F-point, where the vorticity lives
dx_u — float
Metric terms on U-point
dy_v — float
Metric terms on V-point
exchange — callable
Boundary/halo exchange, see module docstring

Output Arguments

field_out — float
Resulting field, on F-points Usage: vort = vort_Vgrid(u, v, e1f, e2f, e1u, e2v, orca.halo)

Example

z = grid_c.vort_Vgrid(u, v, g["e1v"], g["e2t"], g["e1u"], g["e2v"], orca.halo)
z = grid_c.vort_Vgrid(us, 0*us, g["e1v"], g["e2t"], g["e1u"], g["e2v"], orca.halo)
Whole test
with test("orcakit.grid_c.vort_Vgrid"):
    E = []
    for N in (180, 360):
        g = sph(N, N//2); u, v = uv_c(g); pf, lf = g["lat_v"], g["lon_u"]
        ex = (-3*np.sin(pf)*np.sin(3*lf) + 2*np.sin(pf)*np.sin(2*lf))/A
        z = grid_c.vort_Vgrid(u, v, g["e1v"], g["e2t"], g["e1u"], g["e2v"], orca.halo)
        E.append(np.max(np.abs(z - ex)[1:-2]))
    ok("relative error, N=360", E[1]/np.abs(ex).max(), 3e-3)
    ok("order of accuracy minus 2", np.log2(E[0]/E[1]) - 2, 0.2)
    Om = 1e-5; us = Om*A*np.cos(g["lat_t"])
    z = grid_c.vort_Vgrid(us, 0*us, g["e1v"], g["e2t"], g["e1u"], g["e2v"], orca.halo)
    ok("solid-body rotation, against 2 Omega sin(phi)", rerr(z[1:-2], (2*Om*np.sin(pf))[1:-2]), 2e-3)

py-kits › orcakit

mpi_filter

An MPI-parallel spatial filter over a global-ocean 3-D field, using a 2-D horizontal domain decomposition with FULL VERTICAL PENCILS -- every MPI rank owns *all* nz vertical levels but only a rectangular sub-block of the horizontal plane.

Why this shape of decomposition ------------------------------- The motivating operation is a per-level horizontal Gaussian low-pass. Such a filter: * couples neighbouring points horizontally (it IS a horizontal stencil), so a

horizontal split needs halo exchange, but

* does not couple vertical levels (a 2-D Gaussian, sigma_z = 0, is applied

level by level).

Keeping each rank's vertical column whole ("pencil") therefore means the filter never has to communicate in z; all the MPI traffic is a thin horizontal halo.

Two run modes ------------- * NO MPI (`python mpi_filter.py ...`) or `mpirun -np 1 ...`

one rank reads the whole (nz, ny, nx) field and filters it. This is not
a separate code path -- it is the P = 1 corner of the parallel code
(see `Tile.from_whole` / the `cart_comm is None` branches).

* `mpirun -np N ...`, N a perfect square

P = sqrt(N) tiles per horizontal axis, so a P x P grid of ranks. Each
rank reads only its own hyperslab  var[:, j0:j1, i0:i1]  (full depth),
surrounds it with a halo of width  hw = ceil(4*sigma)  filled by
point-to-point exchange with its Cartesian neighbours, filters locally,
and (optionally) the tiles are gathered back to rank 0.

Process grid (example: N = 9, P = 3) ------------------------------------

  cx=0       cx=1       cx=2
+----------+----------+----------+

cy=2 | | | | <- top tile-row = global NORTH edge

|          |          |          |      (tripolar fold)
+----------+----------+----------+

cy=1 | | | | (interior tile-row: ordinary halo

|          |          |          |    exchange on all four sides)
+----------+----------+----------+

cy=0 | | | | <- bottom tile-row = global SOUTH

|          |          |          |      edge (closed)
+----------+----------+----------+
x is PERIODIC: the cx=0 and cx=2 columns are neighbours (E-W wrap).
y is NOT periodic: the cy=0 / cy=2 rows have a real domain edge.

(cy, cx) = cart_comm.Get_coords(rank). With reorder=True the integer rank labels may be permuted by MPI, so we always work from the coords, never from a hand-computed rank number.

Per-rank padded array (`Tile.a`, shape (nz, jl + 2*hw, il + 2*hw)) -----------------------------------------------------------------

                x  ------------------------------------->
     col: 0        hw                     hw+il        hw+il+hw
        +----------+----------------------+----------+
 row 0  |  NW      |      NORTH halo      |     NE   |
        |  corner  |    a[:, 0:hw,        |   corner |
        |          |        hw:hw+il]     |          |
     hw +----------+----------------------+----------+
        |  WEST    |                      |   EAST   |
        |  halo    |      INTERIOR        |   halo   |
        | a[:, :,  |   a[:, hw:hw+jl,     | a[:, :,  |
        |  0:hw]   |       hw:hw+il]      | hw+il: ] |
  hw+jl +----------+----------------------+----------+
        |  SW      |      SOUTH halo      |     SE   |
        |  corner  |    a[:, hw+jl:,      |   corner |
        |          |        hw:hw+il]     |          |
hw+jl+hw+----------+----------------------+----------+

INTERIOR = this rank's own data (jl rows x il cols, all nz levels). halos = width hw, filled by `_exchange` every time we filter. hw = ceil(4*sigma): a Gaussian truncated at 4 sigma reaches exactly

this far, so one halo of this width is all the smoother needs.

Halo / boundary rules (implemented in `Tile._exchange`) ------------------------------------------------------ x : PERIODIC, period nx-2: the last two columns repeat the first two.

Cartesian dim 1 is periodic => every rank always has a valid east and west
neighbour (they wrap); the outermost tiles shift what they send by those
two columns.

y : NON-periodic.

interior tile faces  : ordinary neighbour exchange.
global SOUTH (cy = 0) : closed. South halo = interior rows reflected,
                        the same rule scipy applies in `orca.smooth_2D`.
global NORTH (cy=Py-1): T-pivot fold, as `orca.halo`: the ghosts come
                        from the source row and column of `orca.FOLD`,
                        which depend on the grid point, times fold_sign
                        (-1 for either velocity component, +1 otherwise
                        and for the wet mask). Because each rank holds
                        only part of that global row, the top tile-row
                        pools its strips with an Allgatherv on a row
                        sub-communicator. The corners are filled too.

Expected input layout --------------------- * one netCDF file per (component, date); the netCDF variable name equals the

component name passed on the command line;

* the data variable is 3-D (level, y, x), e.g. (75, 1021, 1442), with no time

axis;

* _FillValue is NaN -> masked_invalid -> data filled with 0 + a separate

0/1 "wet" mask;

* `--meridional` marks a field whose sign flips across the tripolar fold

(either velocity component); by default the fold sign is +1. `--point` says
where the field lives (T, U, V or F).

Sketch-level simplifications -- read before trusting the numbers ------------------------------------------------------------- 1. hw + 5 must be <= the smallest local tile dimension: the halo is filled from

the IMMEDIATE neighbour only (no multi-hop forwarding), and the fold reaches
5 rows further down. This is asserted collectively in `Tile.from_mpi`; if it
trips, use fewer ranks or a smaller sigma.

2. Each rank opens the netCDF independently (no parallel HDF5). That is fine

for read-only access; the (optional) write goes through a gather to rank 0.

Every function docstring below carries a `Called:` line saying whether it is user-facing (you call it from a script / the CLI) or automatic (another routine here calls it), and by whom.

Usage -----

# serial, whole field, cross-check against the reference smoother
python mpi_filter.py --component vozocrtx --date 2015-01-01 --sigma 8 --check

# 16-way (4x4) tiling, gather the result on rank 0 and cross-check
mpirun -np 16 python mpi_filter.py --sigma 8 --check

The gathered result is tiling-invariant and matches the whole-domain reference.

Functions

default_pathPath of the daily file of one variable and date, in this script's data folder.
_splitCut range(n) into p contiguous chunks of nearly equal size.
_read_slabRead all levels of a horizontal window of a variable from disk.
Tile.__init__Low-level constructor; use Tile.from_whole or Tile.from_mpi instead.
Tile.from_wholeA single tile holding the whole field, with its halo filled locally.
Tile.from_mpiThis rank's tile of a P x P decomposition, read as one window of the file.
Tile._exchangeFill the halo of the tile's field or mask, in place.
Tile._north_foldFill the north halo of a padded array from the T-pivot fold, in place.
Tile.smoothLand-aware Gaussian low-pass of this tile.
Tile.gather_to_rootAssemble the tiles of a field into one global array on rank 0.
reference_smoothWhole-domain smoothing in one process, the reference a tiled run is checked against.
mainCommand-line entry point: filter one variable, serial or tiled under mpirun.

default_path

Path of the daily file of one variable and date, in this script's data folder.

Description

The folder and file tag are set at the top of this script.

$$\text{path} = \text{database\_dir}/c/c\_\text{tag}\_\text{date}.nc$$

Syntax

path = default_path(component, date)

Input Arguments

component — str
Variable name, also the folder and file prefix, e.g. 'vozocrtx'
date — str
Date in the file name, e.g. '2015-01-01'

Output Arguments

path — str
The path; no file is opened

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › _split

_split

Cut range(n) into p contiguous chunks of nearly equal size.

Description

Places the tiles of a decomposition in the global grid. The first (n mod p) chunks get one extra cell, as numpy.array_split does: _split(1442, 3) -> [(0, 481), (481, 962), (962, 1442)].

$$n = q\,p + r,\qquad \text{chunk } k \text{ has } q + [k < r] \text{ cells},\qquad \text{start}_k = k\,q + \min(k, r)$$

Syntax

out = _split(n, p)

Input Arguments

n — int
Global size along one axis
p — int
Number of chunks, the tiles along that axis

Output Arguments

out — list
p (start, stop) tuples

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › _read_slab

_read_slab

Read all levels of a horizontal window of a variable from disk.

Description

The field and its wet mask are returned apart because the land-aware smoother averages over wet points only, smoothing the field times the mask and the mask with the same kernel.

$$d = f[:, \text{jsl}, \text{isl}] \text{ with NaN} \to 0,\qquad w = [f \text{ finite}]$$

Syntax

data, wet = _read_slab(path, varname)data, wet = _read_slab(path, varname, jsl=slice(None), isl=slice(None))

Input Arguments

path — str
NetCDF file
varname — str
3D (level, y, x) variable
jsl — slice — default slice(None)
Rows to read, all by default
isl — slice — default slice(None)
Columns to read, all by default

Output Arguments

data — float
(nz, ny_sel, nx_sel) float32 field, NaN and fill as 0
wet — float
Same shape, 1 where the value read was finite, else 0

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › Tile.__init__

Tile.__init__

Low-level constructor; use Tile.from_whole or Tile.from_mpi instead.

Description

Allocates the padded buffers of the field and its mask and fills their interior.

$$a[:, h:h+j_l,\ h:h+i_l] = d,\qquad w[:, h:h+j_l,\ h:h+i_l] = m,\qquad h = \lceil 4\sigma \rceil$$

Syntax

Tile.__init__(data, wet, hw, is_meridional)Tile.__init__(data, wet, hw, is_meridional, point='T', cart_comm=None, Px=1, Py=1, cx=0, cy=0, i0=0, j0=0, ny_g=None, nx_g=None)

Input Arguments

data, wet — float
(nz, jl, il) this tile's field and wet mask
hw — int
Halo width, ceil(4 sigma)
is_meridional — bool
True if the field's sign flips across the fold
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives
cart_comm — Comm — default None
Cartesian communicator, or None for serial
Px, Py — int
Tiles per axis, 1 when serial
cx, cy — int
This tile's column and row in the P x P grid
i0, j0 — int
Global index of its first interior column and row
ny_g, nx_g — int
Global sizes, by default those of data (serial)

Output Arguments

None.

    for nr in (1, 4):

        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › Tile.from_whole

Tile.from_whole

A single tile holding the whole field, with its halo filled locally.

Description

The serial case, also the reference that a tiled run should reproduce.

$$\text{one tile: } (j_0, i_0) = (0, 0),\ (j_l, i_l) = (n_y, n_x),\ h = \lceil 4\sigma \rceil$$

Syntax

tile = Tile.from_whole(path, varname, sigma, is_meridional)tile = Tile.from_whole(path, varname, sigma, is_meridional, point='T')

Input Arguments

path — str
NetCDF file
varname — str
Variable to load
sigma — float
Gaussian lengthscale the tile will be smoothed with, in grid points
is_meridional — bool
True if the field's sign flips across the fold
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives

Output Arguments

tile — Tile

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › Tile.from_mpi

Tile.from_mpi

This rank's tile of a P x P decomposition, read as one window of the file.

Description

Each rank reads only its own part of the field, so a grid too large for one process can be filtered.

Exits the program if the number of ranks is not a perfect square, or if the halo would be wider than the thinnest tile.

$$P = \sqrt{N},\ h = \lceil 4\sigma \rceil \le \min(j_l, i_l),\ \text{tile from \_split}$$

Syntax

tile = Tile.from_mpi(comm, path, varname, sigma, is_meridional)tile = Tile.from_mpi(comm, path, varname, sigma, is_meridional, point='T')

Input Arguments

comm — Comm
MPI communicator of size P*P
path — str
NetCDF file
varname — str
Variable to load
sigma — float
Gaussian lengthscale, in grid points; sets hw = ceil(4 sigma)
is_meridional — bool
True if the field's sign flips across the fold
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives

Output Arguments

tile — Tile
This rank's tile

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › Tile._exchange

Tile._exchange

Fill the halo of the tile's field or mask, in place.

Description

The field and its mask are exchanged with the same pattern, so their halos agree when one is divided by the other; they differ only in the sign at the fold. In serial one tile spans the globe; in parallel each edge comes from the neighbouring tile.

$$\text{as mpi\_orca.exchange\_halo, with sign } s \text{ at the fold}$$

Syntax

Tile._exchange(a, fold_sign)

Input Arguments

a — float
self.a or self.w, (nz, jl+2hw, il+2hw), interior at a[:, hw:hw+jl, hw:hw+il]
fold_sign — float
+1 for a field that does not flip and for the mask, -1 for one that does

Output Arguments

None.

with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › Tile._north_fold

Tile._north_fold

Fill the north halo of a padded array from the T-pivot fold, in place.

Description

Beyond the top row the ORCA grid folds back on itself: each ghost row is a real row further south, read in reverse, with the sign flipped for a velocity component. In parallel the tiles of the top row pool their strips to find the mirrored columns.

$$a_{n_y+p,\,i} = s\;a_{n_y-r-p,\ \mathrm{fold}(i)},\qquad p = 0, \dots, h-1$$

Syntax

Tile._north_fold(a, fold_sign, my_i0)

Input Arguments

a — float
Padded array being filled
fold_sign — float
-1 for a field that flips sign at the fold, else +1
my_i0 — int
This tile's first global column, 0 when serial

Output Arguments

None.

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › Tile.smooth

Tile.smooth

Land-aware Gaussian low-pass of this tile.

Description

The field times the mask and the mask are smoothed with the same kernel and divided, so land does not pull the result towards zero near the coasts.

Where the smoothed mask is below 0.01, almost all land, the result is set to 0, as on land.

$$\tilde f = \frac{G_\sigma * (f\,m)}{G_\sigma * m}\;m \quad\text{where } G_\sigma * m > 0.01,\ \text{else } 0$$

Syntax

field_out = Tile.smooth(sigma)

Input Arguments

sigma — float
Gaussian lengthscale, in grid points; levels are not mixed

Output Arguments

field_out — float
(nz, jl, il) smoothed interior, exactly 0 on land

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › Tile.gather_to_root

Tile.gather_to_root

Assemble the tiles of a field into one global array on rank 0.

Description

Needed to write or check the whole field. It can be a few hundred MB on rank 0, so ask for it only when the whole field is needed.

$$F[:, j_0^{(r)} : j_0^{(r)} + j_l^{(r)},\ i_0^{(r)} : i_0^{(r)} + i_l^{(r)}] = f^{(r)} \quad \text{on rank 0}$$

Syntax

field = Tile.gather_to_root(local)

Input Arguments

local — float
This rank's (nz, jl, il) result, or (nz, ny, nx) when serial

Output Arguments

field — float
(nz, ny_g, nx_g) on rank 0, None on the other ranks; local itself when serial

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_filter › reference_smooth

reference_smooth

Whole-domain smoothing in one process, the reference a tiled run is checked against.

Description

The land-aware ratio is written out so that only the field carries the sign of a velocity across the fold, never the mask: a sign-flipped mask would blow up the ratio on the rows with little ocean just south of the fold. The result does not depend on any tiling.

$$\tilde f = \frac{G_\sigma * (f\,m)}{G_\sigma * m}\;m,\ \text{the field with sign } s \text{ at the fold, the mask without}$$

Syntax

field_out = reference_smooth(path, varname, sigma, is_meridional)field_out = reference_smooth(path, varname, sigma, is_meridional, point='T')

Input Arguments

path — str
NetCDF file
varname — str
Variable to smooth
sigma — float
Gaussian lengthscale, in grid points
is_meridional — bool
True if the field's sign flips across the fold
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives

Output Arguments

field_out — float
(nz, ny, nx) smoothed field

py-kits › orcakit

mpi_orca

ORCA / eORCA global-ocean domain decomposition + halo / communication layer.

This module is ONLY the infrastructure. It cuts a global `(nz, ny, nx)` grid into z-pencils (the full water column over a rectangular horizontal tile), moves the thin overlaps between tiles that a horizontally non-local operation needs, and assembles per-tile results back into a global array. It contains NO grid operations (smoothing, regridding, metric reconstruction, binning, ...) -- those belong in a separate module that imports these primitives.

Serial vs tiled --------------- Every routine takes a `Decomp` as its first argument and branches once on

`dec.serial`:

dec = Decomp.for_file(path, varname)   # serial if no MPI or -np 1,
                                       # else a P x P Cartesian tiling,
                                       # P = sqrt(N)

When `dec.serial` is True the tiled routines fall straight through to the plain whole-array path; when it is a tiled `Decomp` they add exactly the MPI step (halo exchange, a gather, or an allreduce) that a caller's operation needs.

What's here ----------- partitioning

_split                 -- load-balanced 1-D chunking
Decomp                 -- topology, this tile's global window, neighbours

I/O / assembly

read_slab              -- read this tile's hyperslab (all nz levels)
read_slab_with_halo    -- read the hyperslab AND its halo, straight off
                           disk, no communication (only valid for
                           static/read-only source data)
gather                 -- per-tile -> global array on rank 0
Decomp.allreduce_sum   -- sum a per-tile partial result across all ranks

halo primitives (E-W wrap + tripolar north fold + closed south)

tiled  : add_halo / strip_halo / exchange_halo / _north_fold
serial : halo / dehalo   -- whole-array counterpart, imported from orca

Halo / boundary rules (in `exchange_halo`) ----------------------------------------- x : PERIODIC (east-west wrap), period nx-2: the last two columns repeat the

first two. The Cartesian x dimension is periodic, so every rank always
has a real east and west neighbour; the outermost tiles shift what they
send by those two columns.

y : NON-periodic.

interior tile faces  : ordinary neighbour exchange.
global SOUTH (cy = 0) : closed -- the interior rows reflected, the
                        same rule scipy applies in `orca.smooth_2D`.
global NORTH (cy=Py-1): T-pivot fold, as `orca.halo`: the ghosts come
                        from the source row and column of `orca.FOLD`,
                        which depend on the grid point, times fold_sign
                        (-1 for either velocity component, else +1, and
                        always +1 for a wet mask). The top tile-row
                        pools its strips with an Allgatherv on a row
                        sub-communicator, since the fold spans the full
                        global width. The corners are filled too.

Padded local array (what `add_halo` returns) ------------------------------------------- shape = leading_dims + (jl + 2*hw, il + 2*hw) (jl, il = interior sizes) interior a[..., hw:hw+jl, hw:hw+il] -- this rank's own data west halo a[..., :, 0:hw] east halo a[..., :, hw+il:] south halo a[..., 0:hw, :] north halo a[..., hw+jl:, :] NB `add_halo` uses CENTRED padding (a south halo exists); the whole-array `halo()` primitive does not. For exact `halo()` semantics call `halo()`.

Sketch-level simplifications --------------------------- 1. hw + 5 <= the smallest local tile dimension: the halo is filled from the

immediate neighbour only (no multi-hop), and the fold reaches 5 rows further
down. Checked in `add_halo`; raise if violated -- use fewer ranks or a
narrower halo.

2. Each rank opens the netCDF independently (no parallel HDF5) -- fine for

read-only; a caller that writes a result back does so through `gather`
to rank 0.

Usage -----

dec       = Decomp.for_file(path, "vozocrtx")
sub, wet  = read_slab(dec, path, "vozocrtx")     # this tile (or whole grid)
a         = add_halo(dec, sub, hw)               # padded, halo filled
# ... run a horizontally non-local op on `a` (in another module) ...
full      = gather(dec, strip_halo(result, hw))  # (nz, ny, nx) on rank 0

Functions

_splitCut range(n) into p contiguous chunks of nearly equal size.
Decomp.__init__Low-level constructor; use for_file, auto, from_comm or serial_decomp instead.
Decomp.serial_decompThe whole-grid case, one tile spanning the entire grid.
Decomp.from_commA P x P tiling of the grid over the ranks of a communicator.
Decomp.autoThe decomposition suited to how the program was started.
Decomp.for_fileDecomp.auto with the grid size read from a file; the usual entry point.
Decomp.slicesThe window of a global array that belongs to this tile.
Decomp.is_north_edgeWhether this tile touches the global north edge, the fold.
Decomp.is_south_edgeWhether this tile touches the global south edge, which is closed.
Decomp.barrierWait until every rank reaches this point.
Decomp.allreduce_sumElement-wise sum of an array over all ranks.
read_slabRead this rank's window of a variable from disk.
read_slab_with_haloRead this rank's tile and its halo from disk, with no communication between ranks.
read_slab_with_halo.xreadRead the halo'd columns of some rows, in the contiguous runs that wrap across the seam.
gatherAssemble the tiles of a field into one global array on one rank.
_north_foldFill the north halo of a padded array from the T-pivot fold, in place.
exchange_haloFill the halo of a padded array, in place.
add_haloA padded copy of a tile, with its halo filled from the neighbours.
strip_haloThe interior of a padded array, the inverse of add_halo's padding.
py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › _split

_split

Cut range(n) into p contiguous chunks of nearly equal size.

Description

Places the tiles of a decomposition in the global grid, as NEMO splits its domain. The first (n mod p) chunks get one extra cell, as numpy.array_split does: _split(1021, 3) -> [(0, 341), (341, 681), (681, 1021)].

$$n = q\,p + r,\qquad \text{chunk } k \text{ has } q + [k < r] \text{ cells},\qquad \text{start}_k = k\,q + \min(k, r)$$

Syntax

out = _split(n, p)

Input Arguments

n — int
Global size along one axis
p — int
Number of chunks, the tiles along that axis

Output Arguments

out — list
p (start, stop) tuples

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.__init__

Decomp.__init__

Low-level constructor; use for_file, auto, from_comm or serial_decomp instead.

Description

Records where this tile lies in the global grid and in the P x P layout.

$$\text{tile } (c_x, c_y) \text{ covers } j \in [j_0, j_0 + j_l),\ i \in [i_0, i_0 + i_l)$$

Syntax

Decomp.__init__(cart_comm, Px, Py, cx, cy, i0, j0, jl, il, ny_g, nx_g)

Input Arguments

cart_comm — Comm
Cartesian communicator, or None for serial
Px, Py — int
Tiles per axis, both sqrt(N), or 1 when serial
cx, cy — int
This tile's column and row in the P x P grid
i0, j0 — int
Global index of its first interior column and row
jl, il — int
Its interior sizes, rows and columns
ny_g, nx_g — int
Global horizontal sizes

Output Arguments

None.

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.serial_decomp

Decomp.serial_decomp

The whole-grid case, one tile spanning the entire grid.

Description

Code written for tiles then runs unchanged in one process: every routine of this module falls back to its whole-array form.

$$P_x = P_y = 1,\qquad (j_0, i_0) = (0, 0),\qquad (j_l, i_l) = (n_y, n_x)$$

Syntax

dec = Decomp.serial_decomp(ny_g, nx_g)

Input Arguments

ny_g, nx_g — int
Global horizontal sizes

Output Arguments

dec — Decomp
Serial decomposition, .serial True and .cart_comm None

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.from_comm

Decomp.from_comm

A P x P tiling of the grid over the ranks of a communicator.

Description

The grid is cut into P strips in each direction, one tile per rank. The x axis is periodic and the y axis is not, as on the ORCA grids. MPI may renumber ranks, so each tile's position comes from its Cartesian coordinates.

Exits the program if the number of ranks is not a perfect square.

$$P = \sqrt{N},\qquad [j_0, j_0 + j_l) = \text{\_split}(n_y, P)[c_y],\qquad [i_0, i_0 + i_l) = \text{\_split}(n_x, P)[c_x]$$

Syntax

dec = Decomp.from_comm(comm, ny_g, nx_g)

Input Arguments

comm — Comm
MPI communicator of size P*P
ny_g, nx_g — int
Global horizontal sizes

Output Arguments

dec — Decomp
Decomposition for this rank's tile

    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.auto

Decomp.auto

The decomposition suited to how the program was started.

Description

Serial if mpi4py is missing or the job has one process, otherwise a P x P tiling of all ranks, so the same script runs with or without mpirun.

$$\text{serial if } N = 1 \text{ or no MPI, else from\_comm}(\mathrm{COMM\_WORLD})$$

Syntax

dec = Decomp.auto(ny_g, nx_g)

Input Arguments

ny_g, nx_g — int
Global horizontal sizes

Output Arguments

dec — Decomp
Serial or tiled decomposition, chosen from the run

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.for_file

Decomp.for_file

Decomp.auto with the grid size read from a file; the usual entry point.

Description

Saves passing the grid size by hand.

$$(n_y, n_x) = \text{shape of varname}[1:],\ \text{then auto}(n_y, n_x)$$

Syntax

dec = Decomp.for_file(path, varname)

Input Arguments

path — str
NetCDF file
varname — str
Name of a 3D (z, y, x) variable in it

Output Arguments

dec — Decomp
Serial or tiled decomposition for that grid

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.slices

Decomp.slices

The window of a global array that belongs to this tile.

Description

For reading this tile's part of a file or of a global array.

$$\text{jsl} = [j_0, j_0 + j_l),\qquad \text{isl} = [i_0, i_0 + i_l)$$

Syntax

jsl, isl = Decomp.slices()

Input Arguments

None.

Output Arguments

jsl — slice
Rows of the tile; slice(None) when serial
isl — slice
Columns of the tile; slice(None) when serial

with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.is_north_edge

Decomp.is_north_edge

Whether this tile touches the global north edge, the fold.

Description

Tiles on that edge fill their north halo from the fold rather than from a neighbour. Always true when serial.

$$c_y = P_y - 1$$

Syntax

edge = Decomp.is_north_edge()

Input Arguments

None.

Output Arguments

edge — bool
True on the last row of tiles, and always when serial

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.is_south_edge

Decomp.is_south_edge

Whether this tile touches the global south edge, which is closed.

Description

Tiles on that edge reflect their south halo. Always true when serial.

$$c_y = 0$$

Syntax

edge = Decomp.is_south_edge()

Input Arguments

None.

Output Arguments

edge — bool
True on the first row of tiles, and always when serial

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.barrier

Decomp.barrier

Wait until every rank reaches this point.

Description

For lining up ranks, for example before one of them reads a file another has just written. Does nothing when serial.

$$\text{all ranks wait until every rank arrives}$$

Syntax

Decomp.barrier()

Input Arguments

None.

Output Arguments

None.

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › Decomp.allreduce_sum

Decomp.allreduce_sum

Element-wise sum of an array over all ranks.

Description

When several tiles contribute to the same cells, such as the numerator and denominator of an average onto a coarser grid, their partial results must be summed before use. The array has the same shape on every rank. Does nothing when serial.

$$a \leftarrow \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} a^{(r)}$$

Syntax

total = Decomp.allreduce_sum(arr)

Input Arguments

arr — array
Partial result, same shape on every rank

Output Arguments

total — array
Sum over all ranks, reduced in place (on a contiguous copy if needed); arr unchanged when serial

Example

Whole test
with test(*[f"orcakit.mpi_orca.{n}" for n in NAMES], *[f"orcakit.mpi_filter.{n}" for n in FNAMES]):
    for nr in (1, 4):

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › read_slab

read_slab

Read this rank's window of a variable from disk.

Description

Each rank opens the file on its own and reads only its tile; no parallel file system library is needed.

Missing and fill values are returned as 0, with the mask of valid points beside them.

$$d = f[:, \text{jsl}, \text{isl}] \text{ with NaN} \to 0,\qquad w = [f \text{ finite}]$$

Syntax

data, wet = read_slab(dec, path, varname)data, wet = read_slab(dec, path, varname, level=None)

Input Arguments

dec — Decomp
Decomposition; serial reads the whole grid
path — str
NetCDF file
varname — str
3D (z, y, x) variable
level — int — default None
One level, keeping a leading axis of size 1, or None for all levels

Output Arguments

data — float
(nz, jl, il), or (nz, ny, nx) when serial; float32, NaN and fill as 0
wet — float
Same shape, 1 where the value read was finite, else 0

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › read_slab_with_halo

read_slab_with_halo

Read this rank's tile and its halo from disk, with no communication between ranks.

Description

When the data are a file that every rank can open, a slightly wider window can be read in place of exchanging the halo with the neighbours, which is faster in a loop over many files. The same boundary rules as exchange_halo apply: columns wrap with period nx - 2 across the seam, rows below 0 are reflected, and rows beyond the top come from the fold, sign-flipped for a velocity component.

Unlike add_halo, the halo is not limited by the tile size. Missing values are returned as 0, with the mask beside them.

$$a_{j,i} = f_{j,\ i \bmod (n_x-2)} \text{ in x};\qquad a_{-1-p,\,i} = a_{p,\,i} \text{ south (reflection)};\qquad a_{n_y+p,\,i} = s\,f_{n_y-r-p,\ \mathrm{fold}(i)} \text{ north}$$

Syntax

a, w = read_slab_with_halo(dec, path, varname, hw)a, w = read_slab_with_halo(dec, path, varname, hw, is_meridional=False, level=None, point='T')

Input Arguments

dec — Decomp
Decomposition, serial or tiled
path — str
NetCDF file with a 3D (z, y, x) variable
varname — str
Variable to read
hw — int
Halo width; unlike add_halo, not limited by the tile size
is_meridional — bool — default False
True for a field whose sign flips across the fold, either velocity component; only the fold halo is negated
level — int — default None
One level, keeping a leading axis of size 1, or None for all
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives

Output Arguments

a — float
(nz, jl+2hw, il+2hw) float32 field with halo, or (nz, ny_g+2hw, nx_g+2hw) when serial; NaN and fill as 0
w — float
Same shape, 1 where finite, else 0; never sign-flipped

    for nr in (1, 4):
        print(f"   --- {nr} rank(s)")
        for d, e, tol in run_mpi(nr): ok(f"[{nr}] {d}", e, tol)

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › read_slab_with_halo.xread

read_slab_with_halo.xread

Read the halo'd columns of some rows, in the contiguous runs that wrap across the seam.

Description

A helper of read_slab_with_halo: a window crossing the seam is read in up to three contiguous parts.

$$\text{columns } [i_0 - h, i_0 + i_l + h) \bmod (n_x - 2), \text{ read as contiguous runs}$$

Syntax

part = xread(rows)

Input Arguments

rows — slice
Rows to read

Output Arguments

part — MaskedArray
(nz, rows, il+2hw) data

Example

No test of its own; see the routines that call it.

See also

read_slab_with_halo

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › gather

gather

Assemble the tiles of a field into one global array on one rank.

Description

Needed to write a result or check it against a whole-grid computation. The whole field can be hundreds of MB, so gather only when it is needed; choosing a different root for each field spreads the writing across ranks.

$$F[\ldots, j_0^{(r)} : j_0^{(r)} + j_l^{(r)},\ i_0^{(r)} : i_0^{(r)} + i_l^{(r)}] = f^{(r)} \quad \text{for every rank } r$$

Syntax

field = gather(dec, local)field = gather(dec, local, root=0)

Input Arguments

dec — Decomp
Decomposition the tiles were made under
local — float
This rank's (..., jl, il) tile, or (..., ny, nx) when serial
root — int — default 0
Rank that receives the field

Output Arguments

field — float
(..., ny_g, nx_g) on root, None on the other ranks; local itself when serial

Example

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › _north_fold

_north_fold

Fill the north halo of a padded array from the T-pivot fold, in place.

Description

Beyond the top row the ORCA grid folds back on itself: each ghost row is a real row further south, read in reverse, with the sign flipped for a velocity component, as NEMO's north-fold condition does. In parallel the tiles of the top row pool their strips to find the mirrored columns.

$$a_{n_y+p,\,i} = s\;a_{n_y-r-p,\ \mathrm{fold}(i)},\qquad p = 0, \dots, h-1$$

Syntax

_north_fold(dec, a, hw, fold_sign)_north_fold(dec, a, hw, fold_sign, point='T')

Input Arguments

dec — Decomp
Decomposition, serial or tiled
a — float
Padded array, interior at a[..., hw:hw+jl, hw:hw+il]
hw — int
Halo width
fold_sign — float
+1 for scalars, variances and masks, -1 for velocity components
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives

Output Arguments

None.

Example

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › exchange_halo

exchange_halo

Fill the halo of a padded array, in place.

Description

A tile needs a margin of its neighbours' values for any operation that looks at nearby points, such as a filter or a gradient. This fills it as NEMO's halo exchange does: east-west wrap across the seam, copies from the neighbouring tiles, reflection at the closed south edge and the fold at the north.

The same call serves a field or its mask; only the sign at the fold differs. add_halo allocates the padded array and calls this.

$$\text{west/east: wrap with period } n_x - 2;\quad \text{south: } a_{-1-p} = a_p;\quad \text{north: fold};\quad \text{between tiles: copy of the neighbour's edge}$$

Syntax

exchange_halo(dec, a, hw, is_meridional)exchange_halo(dec, a, hw, is_meridional, point='T')

Input Arguments

dec — Decomp
Serial (one tile spans the globe) or tiled (exchange with neighbours)
a — float
Padded array, interior at a[..., hw:hw+jl, hw:hw+il]
hw — int
Halo width
is_meridional — bool
True for a field whose sign flips across the fold, either velocity component
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives

Output Arguments

None.

exchange_halo(dec, a, hw, is_meridional, point)

add_halo | _north_fold

py-kits › orcakit › mpi_orca › add_halo

add_halo

A padded copy of a tile, with its halo filled from the neighbours.

Description

The building block of operations on tiles that look at nearby points, such as a filter: pad, apply, then strip_halo.

The halo comes from one neighbour, and the fold reaches 5 rows further down, so the halo width plus 5 must fit in the smallest tile.

$$a[\ldots, h:h+j_l,\ h:h+i_l] = f,\ \text{halo from exchange\_halo}$$

Syntax

a = add_halo(dec, field, hw)a = add_halo(dec, field, hw, is_meridional=False, point='T')

Input Arguments

dec — Decomp
Decomposition
field — float
(..., y, x) tile, or the whole grid when serial
hw — int
Halo width; hw + 5 must be at most dec.min_tile, since the halo comes from one neighbour and the fold reaches 5 rows further down, else ValueError
is_meridional — bool — default False
True for a field whose sign flips across the fold, either velocity component
point — str — default 'T'
'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F', where the field lives

Output Arguments

a — float
(..., jl+2hw, il+2hw) padded array, interior at a[..., hw:hw+jl, hw:hw+il]

strip_halo

The interior of a padded array, the inverse of add_halo's padding.

Description

Returns a contiguous copy, ready to be gathered or written.

$$f = a[\ldots, h:-h,\ h:-h]$$

Syntax

interior = strip_halo(a, hw)

Input Arguments

a — float
Padded array from add_halo
hw — int
Halo width used

Output Arguments

interior — float
a[..., hw:-hw, hw:-hw], contiguous

py-kits › orcakit

netcdf

Generic NetCDF file utilities not tied to any particular grid or variable naming convention.

Functions

nc_copyStart a new file from parts of another.
write_fieldsWrite arrays to a new file with the dimensions of a grid file.
write_modesWrite DMD modes in the format of NEMO's stochastic noise input (noise_DMDstatistics.nc).
py-kits › orcakit › netcdf › nc_copy

nc_copy

Start a new file from parts of another.

Description

Copies the global attributes, dimensions or variables of a template, typically a domain file, so that new fields can be added with the same dimensions.

The new file is NETCDF3_CLASSIC and replaces any file of that name.

$$\text{dst} \leftarrow \{\text{attributes},\ \text{dimensions},\ \text{variables} \setminus \text{exclude}\} \text{ of src, as selected}$$

Syntax

dst = nc_copy(src_file, dst_file)dst = nc_copy(src_file, dst_file, atts=False, dims=False, vars=False, exclude=['TO_REMOVE'])

Input Arguments

src_file — str
File to copy from
dst_file — str
File to create
atts — bool — default False
Copy the global attributes
dims — bool — default False
Copy the dimensions
vars — bool — default False
Copy the variables and their data
exclude — list — default ['TO_REMOVE']
Variables not to copy

Output Arguments

dst — Dataset
The new file, open for writing; the caller closes it

Example

d = onc.nc_copy(g, os.path.join(TMP, "c.nc"), atts=True, dims=True, vars=True, exclude=["b"]);
Whole test
with test("orcakit.netcdf.nc_copy", "orcakit.netcdf.write_fields", "orcakit.netcdf.write_modes"):
    g = ncfile("grid.nc", dict(z=2, y=3, x=4), a=(("y", "x"), np.arange(12.).reshape(3, 4)), b=(("y", "x"), np.zeros((3, 4))))
    d = onc.nc_copy(g, os.path.join(TMP, "c.nc"), atts=True, dims=True, vars=True, exclude=["b"]);
    ok("variable copied", d["a"][:].data - np.arange(12.).reshape(3, 4), 0); yes("excluded variable left out", "b" not in d.variables); d.close()
    f3 = np.arange(24.).reshape(2, 3, 4); f3n = f3.copy(); f3n[0, 0, 0] = np.nan; f2 = np.ma.array(np.ones((3, 4)), mask=np.eye(3, 4, dtype=bool))
    out = os.path.join(TMP, "w.nc"); onc.write_fields(g, out, dict(p=f3n, q=f2))
    with netCDF4.Dataset(out) as nc:
        nc.set_auto_mask(False); ok("3D field", nc["p"][:][0, 1:] - f3[0, 1:], 1e-5); ok("NaN to fill", nc["p"][:][0, 0, 0], 0); ok("masked to fill", nc["q"][:][0, 0], 0); yes("dims follow the rank", nc["q"].dimensions == ("y", "x"))
    m = (1+2j)*np.ones((2, 2, 3, 4)); out = os.path.join(TMP, "m.nc"); onc.write_modes(out, dict(uavg=f3), dict(umode=m), np.array([.1, .2]))
    with netCDF4.Dataset(out) as nc:
        ok("mean", nc["uavg"][:] - f3, 0); ok("real", nc["umode_real_r"][:] - 1, 0); ok("imag", nc["umode_imag_r"][:] - 2, 0); ok("omega", nc["omega"][:] - [.1, .2], 0)

py-kits › orcakit › netcdf › write_fields

write_fields

Write arrays to a new file with the dimensions of a grid file.

Description

Each array takes the last of the given dimension names that match its rank, so 3D and 2D fields can share one file.

Masked and NaN values are stored as the fill value.

$$\text{dst}[\text{name}] = \text{fields}[\text{name}],\ \text{masked and NaN} \to \text{fill\_value}$$

Syntax

write_fields(grid_file, dst_file, fields)write_fields(grid_file, dst_file, fields, dims=('z', 'y', 'x'), fill_value=0.0)

Input Arguments

grid_file — str
File whose dimensions are copied
dst_file — str
File to create
fields — dict
{name: array}; each array takes the last array.ndim names of dims
dims — tuple — default ('z', 'y', 'x')
Dimension names, outermost first
fill_value — float — default 0.0
Value stored for masked and NaN points

Output Arguments

None.

Example

out = os.path.join(TMP, "w.nc"); onc.write_fields(g, out, dict(p=f3n, q=f2))
Whole test

py-kits › orcakit › netcdf › write_modes

write_modes

Write DMD modes in the format of NEMO's stochastic noise input (noise_DMDstatistics.nc).

Description

The mean fields, the real and imaginary parts of each mode, and their angular frequencies, with the variable names the model reads.

$$\text{prefix\_real\_r} = \mathrm{Re}\,\phi,\qquad \text{prefix\_imag\_r} = \mathrm{Im}\,\phi,\qquad \text{omega} = \omega$$

Syntax

write_modes(dst_file, means, modes, omega)

Input Arguments

dst_file — str
File to create
means — dict
{name: (z, y, x)} mean fields, e.g. {'uavg': ...}
modes — dict
{prefix: complex (modes, z, y, x)}, written as <prefix>_real_r and <prefix>_imag_r
omega — float
(modes,) angular frequencies, in rad/s

Output Arguments

None.

Example

m = (1+2j)*np.ones((2, 2, 3, 4)); out = os.path.join(TMP, "m.nc"); onc.write_modes(out, dict(uavg=f3), dict(umode=m), np.array([.1, .2]))

py-kits › orcakit

orca

ORCA/eORCA-family grid specifics: halo (boundary) exchange including the tripolar north-fold sign flip, 2D smoothing built on that exchange, nearest -neighbour grid search, downsampling, and NEMO mask construction.

`halo`/`dehalo` are the `exchange` callable expected by grid_c.py's operators (interp_UV2T, hDiv_Vgrid, ...).

Functions

_unit_spherePoints on the unit sphere.

py-kits › orcakit › orca › wrap_columns

wrap_columns

Bring column indices outside the grid back onto it.

Description

The last two columns of the ORCA grids repeat the first two, so the grid is periodic with period nx - 2, not nx.

Indices already on the grid are unchanged.

$$i \mapsto i \bmod (n_x - 2)\quad\text{for } i < 0 \text{ or } i \ge n_x$$

Syntax

i_out = wrap_columns(i, nx)

Input Arguments

i — int
Column indices, any shape
nx — int
Number of columns

Output Arguments

i_out — int
Indices in [0, nx); those already inside are unchanged

Example

Whole test
with test("orcakit.orca.halo", "orcakit.orca.dehalo", "orcakit.orca.wrap_columns", "orcakit.orca.fold_columns"):
    ny, nx = 8, 12; f = 1000.*np.arange(ny)[:, None] + np.arange(nx)
    h = orca.halo(f, np.array([1, 0, 1]))
    ok("east ghost = column 2", h[:, -1] - f[:, 2], 0); ok("west ghost = column nx-3", h[:, 0] - f[:, nx-3], 0)
    for ha in ([1,2,1], [0,1,0], [2,0,0], [0,0,2], [3,3,3]):
        ha = np.array(ha); ok(f"dehalo(halo) with {list(ha)}", orca.dehalo(orca.halo(f, ha), ha) - f, 0)
    ok("isMeridional flips the north ghost only", orca.halo(f, np.array([0,1,0]), True)[-1] + orca.halo(f, np.array([0,1,0]))[-1], 0)
    for P, r, c in (("T", 4, 0), ("U", 4, -1), ("V", 5, 0), ("F", 5, -1)):
        ok(f"north ghost source, {P}", orca.halo(f, np.array([0,2,0]), point=P)[ny+1] - f[ny-r-1, (nx+c-np.arange(nx)) % (nx-2)], 0)
    with warnings.catch_warnings():
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore")
        ok("complex field keeps its imaginary part", orca.halo(1j*f, np.array([1,1,1])).imag.max() - f.max(), 0)

fold_columns

The column that the north fold maps each column onto.

Description

At the north fold the grid is mirrored about a pivot, so a column near one end continues as a column near the other. The mirror column depends on the point type: T and V points, U and F points.

Column indices, any shape
nx — int
Number of columns
point — str — default 'T'

Output Arguments

Mirror columns, in [0, nx - 2)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › halo

halo

Add a halo to a field on the ORCA grid, from its own seam and fold.

Description

Operations that look at neighbours, such as filters and differences, need values beyond the edges of the array. On the ORCA grids those are known: east and west, the grid wraps with period nx - 2; north, it folds back on itself about a T-point pivot, as in NEMO, with the sign flipped for a velocity component. This returns the field with that many extra columns and rows filled.

The halo is added at the west, the east and the north; there is none to the south, which is closed. It holds for the fine grids with overlap columns and a T pivot (GLORYS04, GLORYS12, CMEMS), not for eORCA1's domain file, which has neither. The north halo cannot be wider than the rows it mirrors.

$$x_{i,\,n_y+p} = s\;x_{\mathrm{fold}(i),\;n_y-r-p},\qquad s = -1 \text{ for velocity components, } +1 \text{ otherwise},\qquad r \text{ from FOLD}$$
$$x_{i,j} = x_{i \bmod (n_x-2),\,j} \text{ east and west}$$

Syntax

eOrca_haloed = halo(eOrca_field)eOrca_haloed = halo(eOrca_field, halo_array=np.array([0, 0, 0]), isMeridional=False, point='T')

Input Arguments

eOrca_field — float
Field to be haloed, real or complex
halo_array — int — default np.array([0, 0, 0])
np.array([west, north, east])
isMeridional — bool — default False
if True, change the sign of the north halo. Needed by BOTH velocity components, not by scalars or variances
point — str — default 'T'
Where the field lives: 'T', 'U', 'V' or 'F'

Output Arguments

eOrca_haloed — float
Resulting field, at least double precision Usage: halo(t, halo_array=np.array([0,0,1])) halo(u, halo_array=np.array([1,2,1]), isMeridional=True, point="U") halo(v, halo_array=np.array([0,2,0]), isMeridional=True, point="V")

Example

jump = lambda f, m, P: np.median(np.abs(orca.halo(f, np.array([0,1,0]), m, P)[ny, sel] - f[ny-1, sel]))/np.median(np.abs(f[ny-1, sel]))
Whole test
with test("orcakit.orca.halo (fold sign)"):
    W = np.array([0.3, -0.5, 0.2])[:, None, None]
    ei = np.gradient(X, axis=2); ei /= np.linalg.norm(ei, axis=0); ej = np.gradient(X, axis=1); ej /= np.linalg.norm(ej, axis=0)
    u, v = (W*ei).sum(0), (W*ej).sum(0)
    sel = slice(nx//8, 3*nx//8)
    jump = lambda f, m, P: np.median(np.abs(orca.halo(f, np.array([0,1,0]), m, P)[ny, sel] - f[ny-1, sel]))/np.median(np.abs(f[ny-1, sel]))
    print(f"   u: jump {jump(u, False, "U"):.2f} with +1, {jump(u, True, "U"):.2f} with -1;  v: jump {jump(v, False, "V"):.2f} with +1, {jump(v, True, "V"):.2f} with -1")
    yes("-1 gives the smaller jump for u", jump(u, True, "U") < jump(u, False, "U"))
    yes("-1 gives the smaller jump for v", jump(v, True, "V") < jump(v, False, "V"))
    src = open(os.path.join(ROOT, "orcakit/grid_c.py")).read()
    yes("vort_Vgrid exchanges U with the -1 fold sign", 'exchange(Fu, np.array([0, 1, 0]), True, "U")' in src)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › smooth_2D

smooth_2D

Gaussian smoothing in the horizontal, across the ORCA seam and fold.

Description

Smoothing an ORCA field as a plain array would treat the seam and the north edge as walls. Here the field is first padded with its own continuation (halo), smoothed, then cut back, so the filter sees the grid as it really connects.

It does not know about land: land values are averaged in. For a land-aware low-pass use lowpass or masked_smooth.

$$(G_\sigma * f)_{i,j} = \sum_{|m|,|n| \le 4\sigma} \frac{e^{-(m^2+n^2)/2\sigma^2}}{\sum e^{-(m^2+n^2)/2\sigma^2}}\, f_{i+m,\,j+n}$$

Syntax

field_out = smooth_2D(field_in, sigma)field_out = smooth_2D(field_in, sigma, mask=None, isMeridional=False, point='T')

Input Arguments

field_in — float
Field to be smoothed
sigma — float
Gaussian filter sigma, in gridpoints
mask — float — default None
Optional mask applied to the result
isMeridional — bool — default False
if True, change the sign of the north halo
point — str — default 'T'
Where the field lives, see halo

Output Arguments

field_out — float
Resulting field

Example

ok("plane wave against exp(-k^2 sigma^2/2)", rerr(orca.smooth_2D(f, s)[20:-20], (np.exp(-k**2*s**2/2)*f)[20:-20]), 2e-3)
ok("constant preserved", orca.smooth_2D(0*f+5, s) - 5, 1e-12)
s2 = 2.5; ok("non-integer sigma = 2.5 honoured", rerr(orca.smooth_2D(f, s2)[20:-20], (np.exp(-k**2*s2**2/2)*f)[20:-20]), 2e-3)
ok("mask applied", orca.smooth_2D(f, s, mask=mk)[:10], 0)
Whole test

    f = np.cos(k*x)[None]*np.ones((ny, nx))
    ok("plane wave against exp(-k^2 sigma^2/2)", rerr(orca.smooth_2D(f, s)[20:-20], (np.exp(-k**2*s**2/2)*f)[20:-20]), 2e-3)
    ok("constant preserved", orca.smooth_2D(0*f+5, s) - 5, 1e-12)
    s2 = 2.5; ok("non-integer sigma = 2.5 honoured", rerr(orca.smooth_2D(f, s2)[20:-20], (np.exp(-k**2*s2**2/2)*f)[20:-20]), 2e-3)
    mk = np.ones((ny, nx)); mk[:10] = 0
    ok("mask applied", orca.smooth_2D(f, s, mask=mk)[:10], 0)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › _unit_sphere

_unit_sphere

Points on the unit sphere.

Description

Distances between Cartesian points need no special case for the longitude wrap or the poles.

$$\mathbf{x} = (\cos\varphi\cos\lambda,\ \cos\varphi\sin\lambda,\ \sin\varphi)$$

Syntax

xyz = _unit_sphere(lat, lon)

Input Arguments

lat — float
Latitudes, in degrees, any shape
lon — float
Longitudes, in degrees, same shape

Output Arguments

xyz — float
(..., 3) Cartesian coordinates

Example

Whole test
with test("orcakit.orca._unit_sphere", "orcakit.orca.find_nearest_LatLon", "orcakit.orca.find_nearest_grid", "orcakit.orca.load_or_make_map", "orcakit.orca.downsample_field"):
    lat = np.arange(-60., 61)[:, None]*np.ones((121, 360)); lon = np.arange(-180., 180)[None]*np.ones((121, 360))
    ja, ia = orca.find_nearest_LatLon(lat, lon, 10.3, 20.2); ok("regular grid", [ja-70, ia-200], 0)
    ja, ia = orca.find_nearest_LatLon(lat, lon, 0., 179.9); ok("longitude wrap: index of -180", ia - 0, 0)
    latc = np.array([[-10.2, 3.1], [20.4, 40.6]]); lonc = np.array([[-20.3, 50.2], [100.1, 120.4]])
    jm, im = orca.find_nearest_grid(latc, lonc, lat, lon)
    ok("grid lat", jm - (np.round(latc)+60), 0); ok("grid lon", im - (np.round(lonc)+180), 0)
    mk = np.array([[True, False], [True, True]]); jm2, im2 = orca.find_nearest_grid(latc, lonc, lat, lon, mask=mk)
    ok("masked points stay -999", jm2[0, 1] + 999, 0)
    p = os.path.join(TMP, "map.nc"); a = orca.load_or_make_map(p, latc, lonc, lat, lon); b = orca.load_or_make_map(p, latc, lonc, lat, lon)
    ok("map made", a[0]-jm, 0); ok("map reloaded", b[1]-im, 0)
    f = 1000.*np.arange(121)[:, None] + np.arange(360)
    ds = orca.downsample_field(f, jm, im, mk); ok("sampled values", ds[mk] - (1000.*jm + im)[mk], 0); ok("off-mask zero", ds[0, 1], 0)
    d3 = orca.downsample_field(np.stack([f, 2*f]) * (1+1j), jm, im, mk)
    ok("leading axis and complex", d3[1][mk] - 2*(1+1j)*(1000.*jm + im)[mk], 0)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › find_nearest_grid

find_nearest_grid

For each point of a coarse grid, the nearest point of a fine grid.

Description

Sampling a high-resolution field onto a coarser grid needs, for each coarse point, the fine point closest to it. Distances are taken on the sphere, so the seam and the fold need no special case.

The last two fine rows are left out, since they only repeat rows south of the fold. Coarse points outside the mask get -999.

$$\mathbf{x} = (\cos\varphi\cos\lambda,\ \cos\varphi\sin\lambda,\ \sin\varphi),\qquad \text{nearest} = \arg\min_f \|\mathbf{x}_c - \mathbf{x}_f\|$$

Syntax

find_nearest_grid(lat_coarse, lon_coarse, lat_fine_in, lon_fine_in)find_nearest_grid(lat_coarse, lon_coarse, lat_fine_in, lon_fine_in, mask=None)

Input Arguments

lat_coarse — float
Latitude array of the coarse grid
lon_coarse — float
Longitude array of the coarse grid lat_fine_in (float): Latitude array of the fine grid lon_fine_in (float): Longitude array of the fine grid mask (bool): Restrict the search to these coarse-grid points

Output Arguments

None.

Example

jm, im = orca.find_nearest_grid(latc, lonc, lat, lon)
mk = np.array([[True, False], [True, True]]); jm2, im2 = orca.find_nearest_grid(latc, lonc, lat, lon, mask=mk)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › downsample_field

downsample_field

Sample a fine field onto a coarse grid at the nearest fine points.

Description

Each coarse point takes the value of its nearest fine point, from find_nearest_grid. It keeps the fine values unaveraged, so a noisy field stays noisy; coarse_grain averages instead.

Points outside the coarse mask are 0. Leading axes, such as levels, are kept.

$$f^{c}_{j,i} = f^{f}_{\,\mathrm{ilat}_{j,i},\ \mathrm{ilon}_{j,i}} \ \text{where } m^{c}_{j,i},\ 0 \text{ elsewhere}$$

Syntax

field_ds = downsample_field(field_HR, ilat_HR, ilon_HR, mask_LR)field_ds = downsample_field(field_HR, ilat_HR, ilon_HR, mask_LR, nz=None)

Input Arguments

field_HR — float
High-resolution field to sample from
ilat_HR — int
Latitude index array, from find_nearest_grid
ilon_HR — int
Longitude index array, from find_nearest_grid
mask_LR — bool
Low-resolution mask; only True points are filled
nz — int — default None
Unused, kept for older callers; leading axes follow field_HR

Output Arguments

field_ds — float
Downsampled field, field_HR's leading axes + mask_LR's shape

Example

ds = orca.downsample_field(f, jm, im, mk); ok("sampled values", ds[mk] - (1000.*jm + im)[mk], 0); ok("off-mask zero", ds[0, 1], 0)
d3 = orca.downsample_field(np.stack([f, 2*f]) * (1+1j), jm, im, mk)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › create_tmask_from_top_and_bottom

create_tmask_from_top_and_bottom

The 3D T-point mask from the first and last wet levels of each column.

Description

Domain files store only those two levels per column; the mask is 1 between them and 0 elsewhere, as NEMO builds it.

$$t_{i,j,k} = 1 \text{ if } \mathrm{top}_{i,j} \le k \le \mathrm{bottom}_{i,j},\ 0 \text{ otherwise}$$

Syntax

create_tmask_from_top_and_bottom(top, bot, nz, nlat, nlon)

Input Arguments

None.

Output Arguments

None.

Example

t = orca.create_tmask_from_top_and_bottom(top, bot, 3, 3, 3)
Whole test
with test("orcakit.orca.create_tmask_from_top_and_bottom", "orcakit.orca.create_umask_from_tmask", "orcakit.orca.create_vmask_from_tmask"):
    top = np.array([[1, 1, 2], [1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 1]]); bot = np.array([[3, 2, 3], [1, 0, 2], [2, 2, 2]])
    t = orca.create_tmask_from_top_and_bottom(top, bot, 3, 3, 3)
    ok("column (0,2) = 0,1,1", t[:, 0, 2] - [0, 1, 1], 0); ok("land column (1,1) with top=0", t[:, 1, 1], 0); ok("total wet cells", t.sum() - 16, 0)
    t = (np.random.default_rng(1).random((3, 8, 10)) > .3).astype(float)
    ok("umask = t(i) t(i+1), interior", orca.create_umask_from_tmask(t)[:, :, :-1] - t[:, :, :-1]*t[:, :, 1:], 0)
    ok("vmask = t(j) t(j+1), interior", orca.create_vmask_from_tmask(t)[:, :-1] - t[:, :-1]*t[:, 1:], 0)
