py-kits › orcakit › orca › e3uv_from_partial_steps

e3uv_from_partial_steps

U-point and V-point cell thicknesses on a grid with partial cells at the sea floor.

Description

With partial steps, the deepest cell of each column is thinner than its level, to follow the bathymetry. Older mesh files store only the T-point thicknesses; NEMO takes the thickness at a U or V point as the smaller of its two T-cells, which this rebuilds, so transports through the faces near the bottom have the right size.

The deepest wet level of each column comes from the T mask, not from the U or V masks, which already require both neighbours: using them left some wet points with no thickness. The result is 0 on land.

$$e_{3t,k} = e_{3t,k}^{0} \text{ above the deepest wet level},\quad e_{3t}^{ps} \text{ at it},\quad 0 \text{ below}$$
$$e_{3u} = \min(e_{3t,i},\,e_{3t,i+1})\,u,\qquad e_{3v} = \min(e_{3t,j},\,e_{3t,j+1})\,v$$

Syntax

e3u, e3v = e3uv_from_partial_steps(e3t_0, e3t_ps, tmask, umask, vmask)

Input Arguments

e3t_0 — float
(nz,) 1D reference thickness per z-level
e3t_ps — float
(y, x) partial-step bottom-cell thickness
tmask — bool
(nz, y, x) T-point wet mask
umask — bool
(nz, y, x) U-point wet mask
vmask — bool
(nz, y, x) V-point wet mask

Output Arguments

e3u, e3v — float
(nz, y, x) reconstructed cell thicknesses, zero outside umask/vmask respectively Note: bottom_idx (each T-column's own deepest wet level) MUST come from tmask, not from umask/vmask -- umask(k,i,j) already requires BOTH tmask(k,i,j) and tmask(k,i+1,j), so deriving it from umask instead double-applies that condition and can leave e3u spuriously zero at some genuinely-wet U-points. Hit exactly this failure (NaNs from a few zero-weight-but-wet columns) building the first version of this function -- see the GLORYS04 variance notebook's mesh_mask cell for the full failure mode, before it was folded in here. Callees: halo Last check date: 2026-09-05 (earlier noise-generation code)

Example

e3u, e3v = orca.e3uv_from_partial_steps(e0, ps, t, t, t)
Whole test

    ok("V inside A", e3v[:, 1, 0] - [10, 20, 12], 1e-12)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › split_barotropic

split_barotropic

Split a field into its depth mean and the departure from it.

Description

The barotropic part is the same at all depths, the baroclinic part varies with depth and averages to zero over the column. With the cell thicknesses as weights the mean is the true depth mean, as in NEMO's barotropic forcing; without them every level counts equally.

Masked points are left out of the mean, and both parts are 0 on land.

$$\bar u = \frac{\sum_k e_{3,k}\,u_k\,m_k}{\sum_k e_{3,k}\,m_k},\qquad u'_k = (u_k - \bar u)\,m_k$$

Syntax

barotropic, baroclinic = split_barotropic(field_in, mask3d)barotropic, baroclinic = split_barotropic(field_in, mask3d, e3=None)

Input Arguments

field_in — float
(..., k, y, x) field, k = vertical levels
mask3d — float
(k, y, x) wet-point mask (1 valid, 0 for land/below-bottom), broadcastable against field_in
e3 — float — default None
Optional cell thickness, broadcastable against field_in, for a volume-weighted mean; if None, an unweighted mean over wet levels is used instead (an approximation, for when no vertical metric is available)

Output Arguments

barotropic — float
(..., y, x) vertical-mean field, masked
baroclinic — float
(..., k, y, x) field_in - barotropic, masked Last check date: 2026-09-05 (earlier noise-generation code)

Example

f = (B + c)*np.ones((3, 2, 2)); bt, bc = orca.split_barotropic(f, mk, e3=e3)
bt2, _ = orca.split_barotropic(f, mk); ok("unweighted mean", bt2[1, 1] - (B + 1/3), 1e-13)
btt, _ = orca.split_barotropic(np.stack([f, 2*f]), mk, e3=e3); ok("leading time axis", btt[1, 1, 1] - 2*B, 1e-13)
Whole test

py-kits › orcakit › orca › assign_to_coarse_grid

assign_to_coarse_grid

For each fine point, the nearest wet cell of a coarse grid.

Description

The direction opposite to find_nearest_grid: many fine points go to each coarse cell, so a coarse value can be the average of all the fine points inside it rather than one sample. Distances are taken on the sphere, so the seam and the fold need no special case.

Only wet coarse cells receive points. The index refers to the flattened coarse grid.

$$c(p) = \arg\min_{c\ \text{wet}} \|\mathbf{x}_p - \mathbf{x}_c\|,\qquad \mathbf{x} = (\cos\varphi\cos\lambda,\ \cos\varphi\sin\lambda,\ \sin\varphi)$$

Syntax

idx = assign_to_coarse_grid(lat_fine, lon_fine, lat_coarse, lon_coarse, mask_coarse)

Input Arguments

lat_fine, lon_fine — float
fine-grid coords (deg), 2D
lat_coarse, lon_coarse — float
coarse-grid coords (deg), 2D
mask_coarse — bool
coarse wet mask, 2D

Output Arguments

idx — int
shape of lat_fine; values are flat indices into the FULL flattened coarse grid (0 .. lat_coarse.size-1), restricted to wet cells. Pass n_coarse_cells = lat_coarse.size to bin_to_coarse, and reshape a per-coarse-cell array straight back to lat_coarse's 2D shape (land cells just carry count 0). Callees: scipy.spatial.cKDTree Last check date: 2026-09-05 (earlier noise-generation code)

Example

idx = orca.assign_to_coarse_grid(np.array([[0., 0., 0.]]), np.array([[179.5, 9., 11.]]), lc, oc, mk)
idx2 = orca.assign_to_coarse_grid(np.array([[0.]]), np.array([[9.]]), lc, oc, np.array([[True, False]]))
Whole test

    idx = orca.assign_to_coarse_grid(np.array([[0., 0., 0.]]), np.array([[179.5, 9., 11.]]), lc, oc, mk)
    ok("across the seam, then nearest", idx[0] - [0, 1, 1], 0)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › bin_to_coarse

bin_to_coarse

Weighted average of a field over the fine points of each coarse cell.

Description

The averaging half of coarse-graining, once assign_to_coarse_grid has grouped the points.

Cells with no weight get 0, with their weight count 0 beside them. coarse_grain does the same with NaN, any number of leading axes, and the result on the coarse grid.

$$\bar f_c = \frac{\sum_{p:\,c(p)=c} w_p\, f_p}{\sum_{p:\,c(p)=c} w_p}$$

Syntax

avg, counts = bin_to_coarse(field, weight, coarse_flat_idx, n_coarse_cells)

Input Arguments

field, weight — float
(y, x) or (k, y, x); `weight` is the fine wet mask (0/1) or any per-point weight
coarse_flat_idx — int
from assign_to_coarse_grid
n_coarse_cells — int
number of wet coarse cells

Output Arguments

avg — float
(n_coarse_cells,) or (k, n_coarse_cells); 0 where a coarse cell got no weight
counts — float
summed weight per coarse cell, same shape Reconstruct on the fine grid with ``avg[..., coarse_flat_idx.ravel()].reshape(field.shape)``. Last check date: 2026-09-05 (earlier noise-generation code)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › coarse_grain

coarse_grain

Weighted average of a field onto a coarser target grid.

Description

A coarse model cell represents the average of what lies inside it, not one sample of it. Each fine point goes to the coarse cell found by assign_to_coarse_grid, and each cell gets the weighted mean of its points; with cell areas as weights the area integral is kept.

NaN counts as no data, and cells with no weight are NaN. Levels and other leading axes are averaged separately.

$$\bar f_c = \frac{\sum_{p:\,c(p)=c} w_p\, f_p}{\sum_{p:\,c(p)=c} w_p}\quad\text{over points with data}$$

Syntax

field_out = coarse_grain(field, weight, coarse_flat_idx, shape)

Input Arguments

field — float
(..., ny, nx) source field; NaN counts as no data
weight — float
Weights, e.g. cell areas, broadcastable to field; 0 leaves a point out
coarse_flat_idx — int
(ny, nx) flat index of each point's target cell
shape — tuple
(ny, nx) of the target grid

Output Arguments

field_out — float
(..., *shape), NaN on target cells that got no weight

Example

cg = orca.coarse_grain(f_, w_, idx_, (2, 2))
c3 = orca.coarse_grain(np.stack([f_, 10*f_]), w_, idx_, (2, 2)); ok("levels averaged alone", c3[1].ravel()[[0, 1, 3]] - 10*cg.ravel()[[0, 1, 3]], 1e-12)
z_ = orca.coarse_grain(f_, np.where(idx_ == 0, 0., w_), idx_, (2, 2)); yes("zero weight leaves points out", np.isnan(z_[0, 0]))
Whole test

    idx_ = np.array([[0, 0, 1], [1, 3, 3]]); f_ = np.array([[1., 3., 5.], [7., 2., np.nan]]); w_ = np.array([[1., 3., 2.], [2., 5., 9.]])
    cg = orca.coarse_grain(f_, w_, idx_, (2, 2))
    ok("weighted average by hand", cg.ravel()[[0, 1, 3]] - np.array([2.5, 6., 2.]), 1e-13); yes("no weight gives NaN", np.isnan(cg[1, 0])); yes("target shape", cg.shape == (2, 2))
    c3 = orca.coarse_grain(np.stack([f_, 10*f_]), w_, idx_, (2, 2)); ok("levels averaged alone", c3[1].ravel()[[0, 1, 3]] - 10*cg.ravel()[[0, 1, 3]], 1e-12)
    z_ = orca.coarse_grain(f_, np.where(idx_ == 0, 0., w_), idx_, (2, 2)); yes("zero weight leaves points out", np.isnan(z_[0, 0]))

    ja, ia = orca.find_nearest_LatLon(lat, lon, 10.3, 20.2); ok("regular grid", [ja-70, ia-200], 0)
    ja, ia = orca.find_nearest_LatLon(lat, lon, 0., 179.9); ok("longitude wrap: index of -180", ia - 0, 0)
    latc = np.array([[-10.2, 3.1], [20.4, 40.6]]); lonc = np.array([[-20.3, 50.2], [100.1, 120.4]])
    jm, im = orca.find_nearest_grid(latc, lonc, lat, lon)
    ok("grid lat", jm - (np.round(latc)+60), 0); ok("grid lon", im - (np.round(lonc)+180), 0)
    mk = np.array([[True, False], [True, True]]); jm2, im2 = orca.find_nearest_grid(latc, lonc, lat, lon, mask=mk)
    ok("masked points stay -999", jm2[0, 1] + 999, 0)

    ok("map made", a[0]-jm, 0); ok("map reloaded", b[1]-im, 0)
    f = 1000.*np.arange(121)[:, None] + np.arange(360)
    ds = orca.downsample_field(f, jm, im, mk); ok("sampled values", ds[mk] - (1000.*jm + im)[mk], 0); ok("off-mask zero", ds[0, 1], 0)
    d3 = orca.downsample_field(np.stack([f, 2*f]) * (1+1j), jm, im, mk)
    ok("leading axis and complex", d3[1][mk] - 2*(1+1j)*(1000.*jm + im)[mk], 0)

py-kits › orcakit › orca › coastal_taper

coastal_taper

A weight that fades fields towards the coasts.

Description

Fields sampled near land are often unreliable, or would excite spurious responses in a model. This weight is 1 far from land and falls smoothly to 0 at the coast: the mask is smoothed and multiplied back by itself, npass times, each pass pushing the fade further offshore.

It filters all axes of the mask, with no seam or fold handling.

$$\tau_0 = m,\qquad \tau_{n+1} = (G_\sigma * \tau_n)\,m,\qquad n = 0, \dots, n_{\mathrm{pass}}-1$$

Syntax

taper = coastal_taper(mask, sigma, npass)

Input Arguments

mask — array
Wet mask, any shape
sigma — float
Gaussian lengthscale, in grid points
npass — int
Number of passes; more passes push the fade further offshore

Output Arguments

taper — float
float32 weight, 1 far from land, falling towards 0 at the coast, 0 on land

Example

t = orca.coastal_taper(mk, s, 1)[30, 100:130]; d = np.arange(30)
ok("land stays 0", orca.coastal_taper(mk, s, 3)[:, :100], 0)
ok("all-wet stays 1", orca.coastal_taper(np.ones((20, 20)), s, 3) - 1, 1e-5)
Whole test
with test("orcakit.orca.coastal_taper"):
    mk = np.zeros((60, 200)); mk[:, 100:] = 1; s = 6.
    t = orca.coastal_taper(mk, s, 1)[30, 100:130]; d = np.arange(30)
    ok("one pass against the erf profile", t - .5*(1+erf((d+.5)/(np.sqrt(2)*s))), 2e-3)
    ok("land stays 0", orca.coastal_taper(mk, s, 3)[:, :100], 0)
    ok("all-wet stays 1", orca.coastal_taper(np.ones((20, 20)), s, 3) - 1, 1e-5)

py-kits › orcakit

paths

Local data locations, read from paths.toml. See paths.example.toml.

The file is found through the LU_PATHS environment variable, or next to the kits. A location that is not set gives a placeholder path, so importing always works and the error appears only when the data are opened.

Functions

getThe location called `name` in paths.toml.
py-kits › orcakit › paths › get

get

The location called `name` in paths.toml.

Description

Data, meshes and outputs live in different places on each machine. Keeping their locations in one file, outside the code, lets the same code run anywhere.

The file is the one named by the LU_PATHS environment variable, or py-kits/paths.toml. An unknown name returns a placeholder that names it, rather than failing.

$$\text{path} = \text{paths.toml}[\text{name}],\ \text{with } \sim \text{ expanded}$$

Syntax

path = get(name)

Input Arguments

name — str
Key in paths.toml, e.g. 'glorys04'

Output Arguments

path — str
The location, with ~ expanded, or '<name: not set in paths.toml>' if absent

Example

saved = os.environ.get("LU_PATHS"); os.environ["LU_PATHS"] = toml
yes("location read, with ~ expanded", PA.get("one") == os.path.expanduser("~/x"))
yes("unset location gives a placeholder that names it", "two" in PA.get("two") and "not set" in PA.get("two"))

with test(*[f"datakit._source.Source.{m}" for m in ("__init__", "files", "read", "stream", "groups", "mesh", "grid", "vertical", "coords", "depth", "time_hours", "snapshot")], "datakit._source.source", "datakit._source.derived", "datakit._write.write_field", "datakit._write.provenance", "datakit._write.history", "preprocessing.baroclinic.split", "orcakit.grid_c.vertical_velocity", "datakit._source.Source.point_mask", "datakit._source.Source.point_coords", "orcakit.paths.get"):

    toml = os.path.join(TMP, "paths.toml")

    saved = os.environ.get("LU_PATHS"); os.environ["LU_PATHS"] = toml

    yes("unset location gives a placeholder that names it", "two" in PA.get("two") and "not set" in PA.get("two"))

        for n_, a in (("tmask", tm), ("umask", um), ("vmask", vm)): nc.createVariable(n_, "i1", ("t", "z", "y", "x"))[:] = a
        for n_ in ("gphit", "glamt", "gphiu", "glamu", "e1t", "e2t", "e1u", "e2u", "e1v", "e2v", "e1f", "e2f"): nc.createVariable(n_, "f8", ("t", "y", "x"))[:] = 1000.

    lat, lon = np.zeros((ny, nx)), np.zeros((ny, nx)); dep = np.array([5., 20., 45.]); root = S.root
    for i, date in enumerate(("2015-01-01", "2015-01-02")):

    bt_path = WR.write_field(os.path.join(TMP, "stage0_bt"), "v", "2015-01-01", bt, lat, lon, 100., "fk")

py-kits

noisekit

Statistics and structure of the stochastic noise of Location Uncertainty, from ocean data.

In the Location Uncertainty (LU) framework a model is forced by a random velocity whose statistics represent the scales it cannot resolve. noisekit estimates those statistics from high-resolution data: running means, variances and covariances, their change over time, correlation lengths and times, and random fields with a given spatial structure. The pipelines in noisekit.pipelines combine these with the other kits to write the files NEMO reads.

Modules

welfordone-pass mean, variance and covariance, sample by sample, for records too long for memory
runningthe same statistics over a sliding window, to follow how variability changes in time
correlationcorrelation lengths and times by lagged correlation, and their e-folding lags
structurespatially correlated random fields, from an anisotropic diffusion (SPDE) operator
noisegeostrophic velocity from sea level, in its earlier form
pipelinesthe noise methods, each a script from the data to NEMO's input file
py-kits › noisekit

noisekit.pipelines

The noise methods of the catalogue, each a script from the data to NEMO's noise input.

Each pipeline reads a dataset, computes one kind of noise statistic with the kits and writes it in the format tlu_gss.F90 reads. They are kept as they were ported and are being reworked, one by one, into thin wrappers of the kits' routines.

Modules

varianceV1 to V3: constant mean, variance and covariance of u and v

py-kits › noisekit › correlation › efolding_lag

efolding_lag

The lag at which a correlation first drops below 1/e.

Description

The e-folding lag is a simple measure of how far, in space or time, a field stays correlated with itself. The crossing is interpolated linearly between the two lags around it, with lag 0 taken as 1.

Where the correlation never drops below 1/e within kmax, the true lag is at least kmax: it is returned as kmax and flagged as censored rather than given a false precise value. NaN never counts as a crossing.

$$L = (k-1) + \frac{\rho_{k-1} - e^{-1}}{\rho_{k-1} - \rho_k},\qquad k = \min\{k : \rho_k < e^{-1}\},\quad \rho_0 = 1$$

Syntax

L, censored = efolding_lag(rho, kmax)

Input Arguments

rho — float
(kmax, ...) correlation at lags 1 to kmax
kmax — int
Largest lag, returned where there is no crossing

Output Arguments

L — float
(...) e-folding lag, in lag units; kmax where censored
censored — bool
(...) True where rho never crossed 1/e

Example

L0 = 5.5; rho = np.exp(-np.arange(1, 21)/L0)[:, None]; L, c = cr.efolding_lag(rho, 20); ok("L", L[0] - L0, 1.1/(8*L0)); yes("not censored", not c[0])
L, c = cr.efolding_lag(0.9*np.ones((5, 1)), 5); ok("censored at kmax", L[0] - 5, 0); yes("flag", c[0])
L, c = cr.efolding_lag(np.array([[np.nan], [.2]]), 2); ok("NaN skipped, crossing between lags 1 and 2", L[0] - (1 + (0.0)), 1.0)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.correlation.efolding_lag"):
    L0 = 5.5; rho = np.exp(-np.arange(1, 21)/L0)[:, None]; L, c = cr.efolding_lag(rho, 20); ok("L", L[0] - L0, 1.1/(8*L0)); yes("not censored", not c[0])
    L, c = cr.efolding_lag(0.9*np.ones((5, 1)), 5); ok("censored at kmax", L[0] - 5, 0); yes("flag", c[0])
    L, c = cr.efolding_lag(np.array([[np.nan], [.2]]), 2); ok("NaN skipped, crossing between lags 1 and 2", L[0] - (1 + (0.0)), 1.0)

Result in tests/test_all_routines.ipynb:

PASS  L: 2.271e-02 (tol 2.5e-02)
PASS  not censored
PASS  censored at kmax: 0.000e+00 (tol 0.0e+00)
PASS  flag
PASS  NaN skipped, crossing between lags 1 and 2: 0.000e+00 (tol 1.0e+00)

py-kits › noisekit › correlation › spatial_correlation

spatial_correlation

Lagged correlation in space, along x and along y.

Description

The correlation between a point and the point k cells away, over time, measures the spatial scale of a field's variability. Time serves as the ensemble. Several fields, such as u' and v', can be pooled: their lagged products are summed before dividing by their pooled variances.

The fields are taken as anomalies; their mean is not removed. Lags that run off the array are NaN, and points with no variance get 0. Each pair is normalised by the variances at both its ends, which keeps the correlation between -1 and 1.

$$\rho_x(k) = \frac{\sum_f \langle f_{i,j}\, f_{i+k,j} \rangle_t}{\sqrt{\sum_f \langle f_{i,j}^2 \rangle_t \ \sum_f \langle f_{i+k,j}^2 \rangle_t}},\qquad \rho_y \text{ likewise along } j$$

Syntax

rho_x, rho_y = spatial_correlation(fields, kmax)

Input Arguments

fields — list
(nt, ny, nx) arrays
kmax — int
Largest lag, in grid points

Output Arguments

rho_x — float
(kmax, ny, nx) correlation with the point k columns east; NaN where the lag runs off the array, 0 where the variance vanishes
rho_y — float
(kmax, ny, nx) correlation with the point k rows north; same conventions

Example

f = np.cos(k*x[None]+th[:, None])[:, None]*np.ones((nt, ny, nx)); rx, ry = cr.spatial_correlation([f, f], 5)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.correlation.spatial_correlation"):
    nt, ny, nx = 32, 12, 96; k = 2*np.pi*4/nx; th = 2*np.pi*np.arange(nt)/nt; x = np.arange(nx)
    f = np.cos(k*x[None]+th[:, None])[:, None]*np.ones((nt, ny, nx)); rx, ry = cr.spatial_correlation([f, f], 5)
    ok("rho_x = cos(k l)", (rx[:, 2, 10] - np.cos(k*np.arange(1, 6))), 1e-12); ok("rho_y = 1", ry[:, 2, 10] - 1, 1e-12)
    yes("NaN off the end", np.isnan(rx[4, 2, -1]) and np.isnan(ry[4, -1, 3]))

Result in tests/test_all_routines.ipynb:

PASS  rho_x = cos(k l): 2.776e-16 (tol 1.0e-12)
PASS  rho_y = 1: 0.000e+00 (tol 1.0e-12)
PASS  NaN off the end

See also

py-kits › noisekit › correlation › temporal_correlation

temporal_correlation

Lagged correlation in time, point by point.

Description

How long a field stays correlated with itself sets the time scale of its variability, for example the memory of a noise process. The time mean is removed first.

Points with no variance get 0.

$$\rho(k) = \frac{\langle a_t\, a_{t+k} \rangle}{\langle a_t^2 \rangle},\qquad a = f - \bar f$$

Syntax

rho = temporal_correlation(field, kmax)

Input Arguments

field — float
(nt, ...) record
kmax — int
Largest lag, in snapshots

Output Arguments

rho — float
(kmax, ...) correlation at lags 1 to kmax; 0 where the variance vanishes

Example

nt = 20000; om = 2*np.pi/50; a = (3 + np.cos(om*np.arange(nt)))[:, None]; r = cr.temporal_correlation(a, 10)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.correlation.temporal_correlation"):
    nt = 20000; om = 2*np.pi/50; a = (3 + np.cos(om*np.arange(nt)))[:, None]; r = cr.temporal_correlation(a, 10)
    ok("rho = cos(omega l)", r[:, 0] - np.cos(om*np.arange(1, 11)), 2e-3)

Result in tests/test_all_routines.ipynb:

PASS  rho = cos(omega l): 3.766e-04 (tol 2.0e-03)

uv_from_ssh_dAGeostrophic velocity from sea surface height, on interior points only.
py-kits › noisekit › noise › uv_from_ssh_dA

uv_from_ssh_dA

Geostrophic velocity from sea surface height, on interior points only.

Description

The earlier form of orcakit.grid_c.geostrophic_uv, which supersedes it: that one keeps the full grid, leaves land and the equator out, and obeys the seam and fold.

SSH is averaged to F-points with area weights, then differenced onto U and V points, with g = 9.806 and f averaged from T-points. The result covers rows and columns 1 to n-2.

$$U_g = -\frac{g}{f_u}\,\frac{\delta_j \eta_f}{e_{2u}},\qquad V_g = \frac{g}{f_v}\,\frac{\delta_i \eta_f}{e_{1v}},\qquad \eta_f = \frac{\sum_{4} A\,\eta}{\sum_{4} A}$$

Syntax

Ug, Vg = uv_from_ssh_dA(ssh, e1t, e2t, ff_t, dx, dy)

Input Arguments

ssh — float
(..., ny, nx) sea surface height, in metres
e1t — float
(ny, nx) T-cell widths along x, in metres
e2t — float
(ny, nx) T-cell widths along y, in metres
ff_t — float
(ny, nx) Coriolis parameter at T-points, in s-1
dx — float
(ny, nx) e1v
dy — float
(ny, nx) e2u

Output Arguments

Ug — float
(..., ny-2, nx-2) zonal velocity on rows and columns 1 to n-2, in m/s
Vg — float
(..., ny-2, nx-2) meridional velocity, same points, in m/s

Example

Ug, Vg = noise.uv_from_ssh_dA(al*jj*dy, O*dx, O*dy, f0*O, dx*O, dy*O)
Ug, Vg = noise.uv_from_ssh_dA(be*ii*dx, O*dx, O*dy, f0*O, dx*O, dy*O)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.noise.uv_from_ssh_dA"):
    ny, nx = 20, 30; dx, dy = 1e4, 2e4; jj, ii = np.mgrid[:ny, :nx].astype(float); f0 = 1e-4; g = 9.806
    O = np.ones((ny, nx)); al, be = 1e-6, 3e-6
    Ug, Vg = noise.uv_from_ssh_dA(al*jj*dy, O*dx, O*dy, f0*O, dx*O, dy*O)
    ok("eta = alpha y: U = -g alpha/f", rerr(Ug, -g*al/f0), 1e-10); ok("eta = alpha y: V = 0", Vg/(g*al/f0), 1e-10)
    Ug, Vg = noise.uv_from_ssh_dA(be*ii*dx, O*dx, O*dy, f0*O, dx*O, dy*O)
    ok("eta = beta x: V = +g beta/f", rerr(Vg, g*be/f0), 1e-10); ok("eta = beta x: U = 0", Ug/(g*be/f0), 1e-10)

py-kits › noisekit › running › rolling_stats

rolling_stats

Mean and standard deviation over a sliding window of snapshots.

Description

Statistics over a short window follow how variability itself changes in time, for example from season to season. Only `window` snapshots are held at once, so a long record can be streamed.

The standard deviation is the population one, divided by the window length.

$$\mu_t = \frac{1}{W}\sum_{s=t-W+1}^{t} x_s,\qquad \sigma_t^2 = \frac{1}{W}\sum_{s=t-W+1}^{t} (x_s - \mu_t)^2,\qquad t = W-1,\ W-1+S,\ \dots$$

Syntax

rolling_stats(snapshots, window)rolling_stats(snapshots, window, stride=1)

Input Arguments

snapshots — iterable
Arrays of one shape, in time order
window — int
Snapshots per window
stride — int — default 1
Keep one window in every `stride`

Output Arguments

None.

Example

out = list(rolling_stats((k*np.ones(2) for k in range(10)), 4)); yes("window count", len(out) == 7)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.running.rolling_stats"):
    out = list(rolling_stats((k*np.ones(2) for k in range(10)), 4)); yes("window count", len(out) == 7)
    ok("index", [o[0] for o in out][0] - 3, 0); ok("mean", out[2][1] - (5-1.5), 1e-14); ok("std", out[2][2] - np.sqrt(15/12), 1e-14)

PASS  index: 0.000e+00 (tol 0.0e+00)

    ok("variance", next(RN.running_stat(sn, 3))[1] - 2/3, 1e-14); ok("std", next(RN.running_stat(sn, 3, stat="std"))[1] - np.sqrt(2/3), 1e-14)

    ok("covariance by hand: 2 var(x)", cv[0][1][0] - 2*(2/3), 1e-14); yes("NaN in y gives NaN", np.isnan(cv[0][1][1]))
    ok("covariance of x with itself is the variance", next(RN.running_cov(zip(sn, sn), 3))[1] - next(RN.running_stat(sn, 3))[1], 1e-14)

running_cov

Covariance of two fields over a sliding window.

Description

How two components vary together, for example u and v, sets the orientation of variability. The two fields must be at the same points: on the C grid, put U and V on T-points first.

Population covariance, as running_stat's variance. NaN in either field gives NaN.

$$c_t = \frac{1}{W}\sum_{s=t-W+1}^{t} (x_s - \bar x_t)(y_s - \bar y_t)$$

Syntax

running_cov(pairs, window)running_cov(pairs, window, stride=1)

Input Arguments

pairs — iterable
(x, y) arrays of one shape, in time order
window — int
Pairs per window
stride — int — default 1
Keep one window in every `stride`

Output Arguments

None.

Example

cv = list(RN.running_cov(zip(xs_, ys_), 3, stride=2)); yes("covariance windows follow the stride", [i for i, _ in cv] == [2, 4])
ok("covariance of x with itself is the variance", next(RN.running_cov(zip(sn, sn), 3))[1] - next(RN.running_stat(sn, 3))[1], 1e-14)
Whole test

py-kits › noisekit › structure › tensor_field

tensor_field

Diffusion tensor and screening coefficient of an anisotropic correlation.

Description

Random fields with a given correlation length and orientation can be drawn by solving a diffusion-type equation. The tensor stretches correlations along the major axis by (w_maj/w_min)^2 relative to the minor one, rotated by theta, and kappa^2 sets the minor length.

$$D = R(\theta)\,\mathrm{diag}\big((w_{maj}/w_{min})^2,\ 1\big)\,R(\theta)^{T},\qquad \kappa^2 = \frac{8\nu}{w_{min}^2}$$

Syntax

Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, kappa2 = tensor_field(w_maj, w_min, theta, shape)Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, kappa2 = tensor_field(w_maj, w_min, theta, shape, nu=NU)

Input Arguments

w_maj — float
Major length scale, in metres; scalar or (ny, nx)
w_min — float
Minor length scale, in metres; scalar or (ny, nx)
theta — float
Angle of the major axis from x, in radians; scalar or (ny, nx)
shape — tuple
(ny, nx) of the result
nu — float — default NU
Smoothness parameter of the correlation

Output Arguments

Dxx — float
(ny, nx), dimensionless
Dyy — float
(ny, nx), dimensionless
Dxy — float
(ny, nx), dimensionless
kappa2 — float
(ny, nx) screening coefficient 8 nu / w_min^2, in m-2

Example

r = 3.; Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2 = st.tensor_field(3e5, 1e5, 0.7, (2, 2))
ok("theta=0", np.array(st.tensor_field(3e5, 1e5, 0., (1, 1))[:3]).ravel() - [9, 1, 0], 1e-12)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.structure.tensor_field"):
    r = 3.; Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2 = st.tensor_field(3e5, 1e5, 0.7, (2, 2))
    ok("trace", Dxx + Dyy - (r*r+1), 1e-12); ok("det", Dxx*Dyy - Dxy**2 - r*r, 1e-12); ok("kappa2", k2*1e10 - 8, 1e-12)
    ok("theta=0", np.array(st.tensor_field(3e5, 1e5, 0., (1, 1))[:3]).ravel() - [9, 1, 0], 1e-12)

py-kits › noisekit › structure › assemble_A

assemble_A

The sparse system of the correlation operator on a masked grid.

Description

A = kappa^2 M - L, where L is the anisotropic diffusion operator with the tensor of tensor_field and M the cell areas. Solving A x = b for white noise b gives a correlated field. It is discretised with the metrics e1, e2 on any C-grid point type.

Faces towards land or off the box carry no flux; there is no periodic wrap. A is symmetrised, so it is symmetric positive definite.

$$A = \kappa^2 M - \nabla\cdot(D\nabla),\qquad M = \mathrm{diag}(e_1 e_2),\qquad \text{flux through a face} = D\,\frac{e_{across}}{e_{along}}\,\delta$$

Syntax

A, M = assemble_A(Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, kappa2, e1, e2, wet)

Input Arguments

Dxx — float
(ny, nx) tensor component
Dyy — float
(ny, nx) tensor component
Dxy — float
(ny, nx) cross component, centred on the cells
kappa2 — float
(ny, nx) screening coefficient, in m-2
e1 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along x, in metres
e2 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along y, in metres
wet — array
(ny, nx) 1 on water, 0 on land

Output Arguments

A — csr_matrix
(ny*nx, ny*nx) system matrix
M — dia_matrix
(ny*nx, ny*nx) lumped mass matrix, e1*e2 on the diagonal

Example

A, M = st.assemble_A(Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2, d*O, d*O, O)
lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(st.assemble_A(*st.tensor_field(2e5, 1e5, 0.6, (20, 20)), 1e4*np.ones((20, 20)), 1e4*np.ones((20, 20)), np.ones((20, 20)))[0].toarray())
A, M = st.assemble_A(Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2, 1e4*np.ones((n, n)), 2e4*np.ones((n, n)), wet)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.structure.assemble_A"):
    Ls = 2e6; kx, ky = 2*np.pi*3/Ls, 2*np.pi*2/Ls; E = []
    for n in (101, 201):
        d = Ls/(n-1); O = np.ones((n, n)); Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2 = st.tensor_field(2e5, 1e5, 0.6, (n, n))
        A, M = st.assemble_A(Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2, d*O, d*O, O)
        jj, ii = np.mgrid[:n, :n]*d; f = np.cos(kx*ii + ky*jj); Af = (A @ f.ravel()).reshape(n, n)/(d*d)
        ex = (k2[0, 0] + Dxx[0, 0]*kx*kx + Dyy[0, 0]*ky*ky + 2*Dxy[0, 0]*kx*ky)*f
        E.append(np.abs(Af-ex)[5:-5, 5:-5].max()/np.abs(ex).max())
    ok("symbol, relative error, n=201", E[1], 2e-3); ok("order minus 2", np.log2(E[0]/E[1]) - 2, 0.2)
    ok("symmetric", (A - A.T).max(), 1e-20)
    lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(st.assemble_A(*st.tensor_field(2e5, 1e5, 0.6, (20, 20)), 1e4*np.ones((20, 20)), 1e4*np.ones((20, 20)), np.ones((20, 20)))[0].toarray())
    yes("positive definite", lam.min() > 0)
    n = 30; Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2 = st.tensor_field(1e5, 1e5, 0., (n, n)); wet = np.ones((n, n)); wet[10:15, 10:15] = 0
    A, M = st.assemble_A(Dxx, Dyy, Dxy, k2, 1e4*np.ones((n, n)), 2e4*np.ones((n, n)), wet)
    ok("A 1 = kappa2 e1 e2 with no-flux land", (A @ np.ones(n*n)) / (k2[0, 0]*2e8) - 1, 1e-10)
    ok("mass matrix", M.diagonal() - 2e8, 0)

py-kits › noisekit › structure › pcg_jacobi

pcg_jacobi

Conjugate gradients with a Jacobi (diagonal) preconditioner.

Description

An iterative solver for symmetric positive definite systems, such as the correlation operator, that needs only products with the matrix.

$$x_{k+1} = x_k + \alpha_k p_k,\quad r_{k+1} = r_k - \alpha_k A p_k,\quad z = P^{-1} r,\quad p_{k+1} = z_{k+1} + \beta_k p_k$$

Syntax

x, hist = pcg_jacobi(A, b, Pinv)x, hist = pcg_jacobi(A, b, Pinv, tol=1e-10, maxit=5000)

Input Arguments

A — matrix
Symmetric positive definite system
b — float
Right-hand side
Pinv — float
Inverse of the diagonal preconditioner, same shape as b
tol — float — default 1e-10
Stop when |r| / |b| falls below this
maxit — int — default 5000
Largest number of iterations

Output Arguments

x — float
Solution
hist — list
Relative residual |r| / |b| after each iteration

Example

x, h = st.pcg_jacobi(A, b, P, tol=1e-10); ok("PCG", rerr(x, xs), 1e-7); yes("PCG reached tolerance", h[-1] < 1e-10)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.structure.pcg_jacobi", "noisekit.structure.cheby_jacobi"):
    n = 25; O = np.ones((n, n)); A, _ = st.assemble_A(*st.tensor_field(2e5, 1e5, .4, (n, n)), 2e4*O, 2e4*O, O)
    xs = np.random.default_rng(1).standard_normal(n*n); b = A @ xs; P = 1/A.diagonal()
    x, h = st.pcg_jacobi(A, b, P, tol=1e-10); ok("PCG", rerr(x, xs), 1e-7); yes("PCG reached tolerance", h[-1] < 1e-10)
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(np.diag(P) @ A.toarray()).real
    x, h = st.cheby_jacobi(A, b, P, ev.min(), ev.max(), tol=1e-10); ok("Chebyshev", rerr(x, xs), 1e-7); yes("Chebyshev reached tolerance", h[-1] < 1e-10)

py-kits › noisekit › structure › cheby_jacobi

cheby_jacobi

Chebyshev iteration with a Jacobi preconditioner.

Description

Unlike conjugate gradients, it needs no inner products, only one matrix-vector product per step, so it parallelises without global reductions. It needs bounds of the preconditioned spectrum instead.

$$x_k = x_{k-1} + d_k,\quad d_{k+1} = \rho_k\rho_{k+1}\, d_k + \frac{2\rho_{k+1}}{\delta}\, P^{-1} r_k,\quad \theta = \tfrac{\lambda_{max}+\lambda_{min}}{2},\ \delta = \tfrac{\lambda_{max}-\lambda_{min}}{2}$$

Syntax

x, hist = cheby_jacobi(A, b, Pinv, lam_min, lam_max)x, hist = cheby_jacobi(A, b, Pinv, lam_min, lam_max, tol=1e-10, maxit=5000)

Input Arguments

A — matrix
Symmetric positive definite system
b — float
Right-hand side
Pinv — float
Inverse of the diagonal preconditioner, same shape as b
lam_min — float
Lower bound of the eigenvalues of Pinv A
lam_max — float
Upper bound of the eigenvalues of Pinv A
tol — float — default 1e-10
Stop when |r| / |b| falls below this
maxit — int — default 5000
Largest number of iterations

Output Arguments

x — float
Solution
hist — list
Relative residual |r| / |b| after each iteration

Example

x, h = st.cheby_jacobi(A, b, P, ev.min(), ev.max(), tol=1e-10); ok("Chebyshev", rerr(x, xs), 1e-7); yes("Chebyshev reached tolerance", h[-1] < 1e-10)
Whole test

    n = 25; O = np.ones((n, n)); A, _ = st.assemble_A(*st.tensor_field(2e5, 1e5, .4, (n, n)), 2e4*O, 2e4*O, O)
    xs = np.random.default_rng(1).standard_normal(n*n); b = A @ xs; P = 1/A.diagonal()
    x, h = st.pcg_jacobi(A, b, P, tol=1e-10); ok("PCG", rerr(x, xs), 1e-7); yes("PCG reached tolerance", h[-1] < 1e-10)
    ev = np.linalg.eigvals(np.diag(P) @ A.toarray()).real
    x, h = st.cheby_jacobi(A, b, P, ev.min(), ev.max(), tol=1e-10); ok("Chebyshev", rerr(x, xs), 1e-7); yes("Chebyshev reached tolerance", h[-1] < 1e-10)

build_filter

Factorise the correlation operator once, for many draws.

Description

Drawing many correlated fields with the same structure only needs the factorisation once; each draw is then a cheap solve.

$$LU = A(w_{maj}, w_{min}, \theta)$$

Syntax

lu = build_filter(w_maj, w_min, theta, e1, e2, wet)

Input Arguments

w_maj — float
Major length scale, in metres; scalar or (ny, nx)
w_min — float
Minor length scale, in metres; scalar or (ny, nx)
theta — float
Angle of the major axis from x, in radians; scalar or (ny, nx)
e1 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along x, in metres
e2 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along y, in metres
wet — array
(ny, nx) 1 on water, 0 on land

Output Arguments

lu — SuperLU
LU factorisation of A, see assemble_A

Example

n = 181; d = 2e4; O = np.ones((n, n)); w = 2e5; lu = st.build_filter(w, w, 0., d*O, d*O, O); kap = np.sqrt(8)/w
dd = 1e4; n2 = 181; O2 = np.ones((n2, n2)); lu2 = st.build_filter(3e5, 1e5, np.pi/4, dd*O2, dd*O2, O2); c = n2//2
Whole test
with test("noisekit.structure.build_filter", "noisekit.structure.draw", "noisekit.structure.unit_variance_scale"):
    n = 181; d = 2e4; O = np.ones((n, n)); w = 2e5; lu = st.build_filter(w, w, 0., d*O, d*O, O); kap = np.sqrt(8)/w
    c = n//2; e = np.zeros(n*n); e[c*n+c] = 1; C = lu.solve((d*d)*lu.solve(e)).reshape(n, n)
    ok("variance against 1/(4 pi kappa^2), relative", C[c, c]*4*np.pi*kap*kap - 1, 0.08)
    for ell in (5, 10, 20):
        rr = kap*ell*d; ok(f"correlation at {ell} cells against kr K1(kr)", C[c, c+ell]/C[c, c] - rr*k1(rr), 0.02)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(2); S = st.unit_variance_scale(lu, d*O, d*O, O, rng, samples=128)
    ok("MC std against exact", np.median(S[60:-60, 60:-60])/np.sqrt(C[c, c]) - 1, 0.1)
    sm = st.draw(lu, d*O, d*O, O, rng); yes("draw has the grid's shape", sm.shape == (n, n))
    dd = 1e4; n2 = 181; O2 = np.ones((n2, n2)); lu2 = st.build_filter(3e5, 1e5, np.pi/4, dd*O2, dd*O2, O2); c = n2//2
    e = np.zeros(n2*n2); e[c*n2+c] = 1; C2 = lu2.solve(dd*dd*lu2.solve(e)).reshape(n2, n2)
    yes("long axis along theta = 45 degrees", C2[c+15, c+15] > 2*C2[c-15, c+15])

py-kits › noisekit › structure › draw

draw

One spatially correlated random field.

Description

White noise is scaled by sqrt(e1 e2), so the result does not depend on the cell size, and passed through the factorised operator.

The variance of the result varies in space; unit_variance_scale gives the factor to make it 1.

$$x = A^{-1}\big(\sqrt{e_1 e_2}\ \xi\big),\qquad \xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$$

Syntax

field = draw(lu, e1, e2, wet, rng)

Input Arguments

lu — SuperLU
From build_filter
e1 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along x, in metres
e2 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along y, in metres
wet — array
(ny, nx) 1 on water, 0 on land
rng — Generator
numpy random generator

Output Arguments

field — float
(ny, nx) correlated field, 0 on land; its variance varies in space, see unit_variance_scale

py-kits › noisekit › structure › unit_variance_scale

unit_variance_scale

Pointwise standard deviation of the draws, by Monte Carlo.

Description

Near coasts and where the grid changes, draws have more or less variance than elsewhere. Dividing draws by this scale makes their variance 1 everywhere, so their amplitude can be set by another field.

Points with almost no variance, such as land, get 1.

$$s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} x_n^2}$$

Syntax

scale = unit_variance_scale(lu, e1, e2, wet, rng)scale = unit_variance_scale(lu, e1, e2, wet, rng, samples=128)

Input Arguments

lu — SuperLU
From build_filter
e1 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along x, in metres
e2 — float
(ny, nx) cell widths along y, in metres
wet — array
(ny, nx) 1 on water, 0 on land
rng — Generator
numpy random generator
samples — int — default 128
Number of draws

Output Arguments

scale — float
(ny, nx) standard deviation; 1 where it is below 1e-8, e.g. on land

Example

py-kits › noisekit

welford

One-pass (online) mean/variance/covariance accumulation via Welford's algorithm. Works array-wise: every aggregate entry is a full field (e.g. shape (nlev, nlat, nlon)), updated in place sample-by-sample, so this never needs to hold the whole time series in memory at once.

Functions

Welford_mean_aggregate_initA fresh (count, mean) aggregate for a running mean.
Welford_meanAdd one sample to a running mean.
Welford_mean_finalizeThe mean of a (count, mean) aggregate.
Welford_aggregate_initA fresh (count, mean, M2) aggregate for a running variance.
Welford_varianceAdd one sample to a running mean and variance.
Welford_finalizeMean, population variance and sample variance of a (count, mean, M2) aggregate.
Welford_aggregate_xy_initA fresh aggregate for the running means, variances and covariance of two fields.
Welford_covarianceAdd one pair of samples to a running mean, variance and covariance.
Welford_cov_finalizeMeans, population variances and covariance of a joint aggregate.

py-kits › noisekit › welford › Welford_covariance

Welford_covariance

Add one pair of samples to a running mean, variance and covariance.

Description

The covariance update uses the mean of x before and of y after the update, which keeps it exact.

$$n \leftarrow n+1,\quad \delta_x = x - \mu_x,\quad \mu_x \leftarrow \mu_x + \tfrac{\delta_x}{n},\quad \mu_y \leftarrow \mu_y + \tfrac{y - \mu_y}{n},\quad C_{xy} \leftarrow C_{xy} + \delta_x\,(y - \mu_y)$$

Syntax

aggregate = Welford_covariance(previous_aggregate_xy, new_sample_x, new_sample_y)

Input Arguments

previous_aggregate_xy — tuple
(count, mean_x, mean_y, M2x, M2y, C2xy)
new_sample_x — float
next sample field for x
new_sample_y — float
next sample field for y

Output Arguments

aggregate — tuple
updated (count, mean_x, mean_y, M2x, M2y, C2xy)

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines

pipelines.build_baroclinic_daily

Standalone MPI batch job: write a per-day, full-depth copy of the GLORYS04 u / v daily snapshots with the BAROTROPIC (transport-weighted depth-mean) component removed.

u_bc(x, z, t) = u(x, z, t) - ubar(x, t),
ubar          = sum_k u * e3u / sum_k e3u          (per water column)

and likewise for v with e3v. ubar is the vertical-mean flow; u_bc carries zero net transport by construction.

Output tree (a sibling of the source daily/ tree, identical layout, dimensions, variable names, coordinates, dtype and _FillValue -- a drop-in replacement any GLORYS04-reading pipeline can point database_dir at):

<storage>/data-OPeNDAP-Mercator/glorys04/daily-baroclinic/
    vozocrtx/vozocrtx_glorys04_YYYY-MM-DD.nc
    vomecrty/vomecrty_glorys04_YYYY-MM-DD.nc

Land and below-seafloor cells are NaN (matching the source _FillValue).

Vertical metric: e3u, e3v are reconstructed from the old-format GLORYS2V4 mesh_mask (T-point e3t_0 + e3t_ps + tmask only, no 3-D e3) via orca.e3uv_from_partial_steps -- the same helper the build_noise_*_stats.py scripts use. The barotropic split itself is orca.split_barotropic.

Parallelism (mpi4py): the day list is split round-robin across ranks; each rank reads, computes and writes its own files independently -- no two ranks touch the same output file, so plain (serial-per-file) netCDF writes are enough, no parallel HDF5. Each output is written to "<name>.tmp<rank>" then os.replace()d into place, so an interrupted run is safely resumable (existing outputs are skipped unless --overwrite).

Every rank independently reads the mesh_mask and rebuilds e3u/e3v (~1-2 s, one 660 MB read served from page cache after the first). Peak memory per rank is ~3-4 GB (e3u_3d + e3v_3d + a full-depth working column for u and v), so keep -np below node_RAM_GB / 4.

Run:

# one-time, into the project venv (openmpi 4.1.6 mpicc is on PATH):
MPICC=$(command -v mpicc)       pip install mpi4py

mpirun -np 16       python -m noisekit.pipelines.build_baroclinic_daily

# options: --overwrite  --years 2015,2016  --limit N  --dst PATH  --dry-run

Full 2 years (731 days x u+v, full 75 levels): ~15 s/day serial (read 2x ~2.3 s + split + write 2x zlib), so ~3 h on 1 rank, ~12 min on 16 ranks. ~250-300 GB of output (source dtype is float64).

Prototyped in the GLORYS04 variance notebook ("Remove the barotropic mode" section); this is that operation over the whole archive, in parallel, with the result persisted as a dataset instead of held in RAM.

Example

Whole test
with test("noisekit.pipelines.build_baroclinic_daily.log", "noisekit.pipelines.build_baroclinic_daily.discover_pairs", "noisekit.pipelines.build_baroclinic_daily.build_metric", "noisekit.pipelines.build_baroclinic_daily.baroclinic_field", "noisekit.pipelines.build_baroclinic_daily.clone_with"):
    ns = load_funcs("noisekit/pipelines/build_baroclinic_daily.py", ("log", "discover_pairs", "build_metric", "baroclinic_field", "clone_with"), np=np, netcdf=netCDF4, os=os, glob=glob, time=time, sys=sys, orca=orca, acc_dtype=np.float32, rank=0, size=1, database_dir=dd, udate_re=__import__("re").compile(r"vozocrtx_glorys04_(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})\.nc$"))
    ns["log"]("hello"); yes("pairs", len(ns["discover_pairs"]("all")) == 2); yes("year filter", len(ns["discover_pairs"]("2014")) == 0)
    mm2 = os.path.join(TMP, "mm2.nc")
    with netCDF4.Dataset(mm2, "w") as nc:
        for d, s in (("t", 1), ("z", 2), ("y", 5), ("x", 4)): nc.createDimension(d, s)
        nc.createVariable("e3t_0", "f4", ("t", "z"))[...] = [[1., 3.]]; nc.createVariable("e3t_ps", "f4", ("t", "y", "x"))[...] = 3*np.ones((1, 5, 4))
        for m_ in ("tmask", "umask", "vmask"): nc.createVariable(m_, "f4", ("t", "z", "y", "x"))[...] = np.ones((1, 2, 5, 4))
    ns["mesh_mask_file"] = mm2; e3u5, e3v5, um5, vm5 = ns["build_metric"](); ok("e3u", e3u5[:, 1, 1] - [1, 3], 1e-6)
    src = os.path.join(TMP, "src.nc")
    with netCDF4.Dataset(src, "w") as nc:
        nc.setncattr("title", "T"); nc.createDimension("z", 2); nc.createDimension("y", 5); nc.createDimension("x", 4)
        v = nc.createVariable("q", "f4", ("z", "y", "x"), fill_value=1e20, zlib=True); v[...] = np.array([4., 8.])[:, None, None]*np.ones((2, 5, 4)); v.units = "m/s"; nc.createVariable("keep", "f4", ("y",))[:] = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    mk5 = np.ones((2, 5, 4), bool); mk5[:, 0, 0] = False
    bc = ns["baroclinic_field"](src, "q", e3u5, mk5); ok("u - sum(u e3)/sum(e3): mean 7", bc[:, 1, 1] - [-3, 1], 1e-5); yes("land NaN", np.isnan(bc[:, 0, 0]).all())
    dst = os.path.join(TMP, "dst.nc"); ns["clone_with"](src, dst, "q", bc)
    with netCDF4.Dataset(dst) as nc:
        ok("field replaced", nc["q"][:, 1, 1] - [-3, 1], 1e-5); ok("other variable kept", nc["keep"][:] - [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 0); yes("attributes kept", nc.title == "T" and nc["q"].units == "m/s")

baroclinic_field

The baroclinic part of one daily velocity file.

Description

The velocity minus its thickness-weighted depth mean. NaN on land and below the sea floor.

$$u' = u - \frac{\sum_k e_{3,k} u_k}{\sum_k e_{3,k}}$$

Syntax

bc = baroclinic_field(src_path, varname, e3, mask3d)

Input Arguments

src_path — str
Daily file
varname — str
'vozocrtx' or 'vomecrty'
e3 — float
(nz, ny, nx) thicknesses at the field's points
mask3d — bool
(nz, ny, nx) wet mask at the field's points

Output Arguments

bc — float
(nz, ny, nx) field minus its e3-weighted depth mean; NaN on land and below the sea floor

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines

pipelines.build_noise_BcResid_stats

Production script: the "barotropic-removed coarse-graining residual" noise statistics for TLU. For every day of GLORYS04 u/v over the full 2-year archive (731 days, gap-free), at the full 75-level column:

1. read u, v in full
2. split off the barotropic mode (e3-weighted vertical mean, via
   orca.split_barotropic + orca.e3uv_from_partial_steps) and KEEP the
   baroclinic part u_bc, v_bc
3. coarse-grain each level of u_bc / v_bc onto the ORCA1 grid:
   Gaussian pre-smooth (sigma_cg gridpoints, representing ORCA1's own
   effective truncation) -> nearest-cell bin-average onto ORCA1 cells
   (orca.assign_to_coarse_grid / orca.bin_to_coarse) -> reconstruct on
   the fine grid.  The RESIDUAL = u_bc - that is the sub-ORCA1-scale
   baroclinic variability -- the target for the TLU sigma*dB_t term.
4. fold the residual into a running Welford mean/variance accumulator
   (one day resident at a time -- 731 days x 75 levels will not stack)
5. downsample the mean/variance fields onto the ORCA1 grid (bin-average
   the fine-grid statistic over each ORCA1 cell's fine points)
6. write noise_BcResid_stats.nc (an nc_copy of the ORCA1 domain_cfg.nc,
   dimensions only, + the 4 fields ubc_resid_{mean,var}, vbc_resid_{mean,var})

Prototyped and step-by-step verified in glorys04-varnoise.ipynb (the "Splitting GLORYS04 into an ORCA1-comparable resolved part" section and the "Barotropic-removed residual" section); this is the same operation run over the full 2 years at full depth.

sigma_cg = 8 GLORYS04 gridpoints: the *global* crossover between resolved and residual variance found in the notebook. It is NOT uniform with latitude (equatorial ~9, mid-latitude ~3-5, high-latitude ~7-13) -- a latitude/space-dependent sigma is deliberately PARKED for now; see the notebook and the tlu-regional-sigma-parked memory note.

DESEASONALIZE (below) is False: this computes the RAW residual mean/variance. The notebook's year-long analysis flagged that an annual+ time-variance folds in the seasonal cycle (a predictable signal, not noise) and should "almost certainly be deseasonalized first" -- doing that properly needs a two-pass structure (pass 1: per-calendar-month climatology of the residual; pass 2: Welford variance of the anomaly). Not implemented here yet -- a flagged, obvious next step.

Memory: full-depth day ~450MB (float64) / ~225MB (float32) per component. Welford aggregates (u/v residual, each mean+M2 at 75 x 1021 x 1442, float32) ~1.8GB total; peak with per-day working arrays a few GB. NOT the ~150GB+ a stack-then-reduce would need.

Runtime: the batched 75-level smooth is ~9 s/component/day; ~23 s/day for both -> order 4-5 hours over the full 2 years. A deliberate batch job, not something to trigger by editing this file.

bc_residual

One day's baroclinic velocity minus its coarse-grained version, on the fine grid.

Description

The part of the baroclinic flow that a 1-degree model cannot represent: each level is smoothed, averaged over the fine points of each eORCA1 cell, put back on the fine grid and subtracted.

$$r = \big(u' - \mathcal{P}\,\overline{G * u'}^{\,\text{cell}}\big)\, m,\qquad u' = u - \bar u^{z}$$

Syntax

residual = bc_residual(path, varname, e3, wetmask_f, smoother, smoother_mask)

path — str
Daily file
varname — str
'vozocrtx' or 'vomecrty'
e3 — float
(nz, ny, nx) thicknesses at the field's points
wetmask_f — float
(nz, ny, nx) fine-grid wet mask
smoother — callable
Smoothing of the field
smoother_mask — callable
Smoothing of the mask, without sign flip

Output Arguments

residual — float
(nz, ny, nx) sub-eORCA1 residual, 0 on land

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines

pipelines.build_noise_lscale

MPI-tiled production script: measure the REAL spatial correlation length of GLORYS04's barotropic-removed, high-passed velocity residual (the same residual build_noise_sigma.py computes the amplitude of) and write it as noise_lscale.nc -- the length-scale/anisotropy counterpart of noise_sigma.nc, per the noise-generation design notes, sec 4.2.7 ("OFFLINE -- build_noise_lscale.py").

Method: time as the ensemble dimension, at each FIXED spatial lag ----------------------------------------------------------------- The design notes, sec 4.1, measured Lx/Ly by pooling a 2-point spatial correlation over a region box -- a few large boxes, not a per-gridpoint map. A naive per-gridpoint version of that (a small spatial sliding window centred on each point) would be poorly sampled (~2*halfwidth independent values per estimate) and would mix together whatever physical regimes fall inside that one window.

Instead: for a fixed spatial lag k, the quantity

rho_x(k; i,j) = < u'(i,j,t) u'(i+k,j,t) >_t  /  < u'(i,j,t)^2 >_t

is a genuine per-gridpoint statistic, averaged over the WHOLE archive (365+ independent days) at that one fixed pair of points -- far better sampled, and it reuses build_noise_sigma.py's exact day-loop/halo-read machinery almost unchanged. The halo already read for the Gaussian high-pass (hw=ceil(4*sigma_hp)=32) is *more* than the lag range this script needs (kmax~25) -- so lagged correlation costs no extra disk I/O or MPI traffic beyond what build_noise_sigma.py already pays per day; see highpass_tile(..., margin=kmax) (a small additive extension to that function, backward compatible -- margin=0 there still means exactly what it always meant).

u' and v' are pooled together (not treated as two separate length-scale maps): the actual thing being measured is the spatial scale of the underlying eddy STREAMFUNCTION (the design notes' sec 4.2 curl-of- streamfunction construction) -- both u' and v' are projections of the SAME scalar field, so pooling their lagged products before dividing (rather than computing Lx from u' and v' separately and averaging two already-independent ratios) is the statistically coherent thing to do, not just a convenience.

2-D, not 3-D: this is the length scale of the CONSTRUCTION operator's smoothing, applied to a 2-D streamfunction -- unlike noise_sigma.nc's u_tvar/v_tvar (a 3-D amplitude field), the design notes' own pseudocode for w_x/w_y (sec 4.2.7 step 2) has no z index. So this script only ever touches the SURFACE level (mpi_orca.read_slab_with_halo(..., level=0)) -- 75x cheaper than build_noise_sigma.py's full-depth day loop, which is why this can comfortably run over the full 2-year archive rather than one year.

Known limitation (documented, not fixed): a coastal wet cell whose k-lag neighbour is on land gets rho_x/rho_y artificially pulled toward 0 at that lag (the neighbour's high-pass residual is exactly 0 there, not "unknown"), biasing the measured length scale short in a narrow coastal band. A properly wet-pair-weighted estimator (numerator/denominator accumulated separately, masked_smooth-style) would fix this; not implemented here -- the bias is narrow-band and this project has accepted comparable edge simplifications elsewhere (e.g. Step G/Step H's Neumann-not-fold boundary in the Chebyshev-Jacobi prototype notebook).

Functions

check_tilingPrint a summary of the lag correlations on rank 0, to compare a serial and a tiled run.

write_noise_lscale.to_orca1Average a 2D fine-grid field over the GLORYS04 points of each eORCA1 cell.
py-kits › noisekit › pipelines.build_noise_lscale › accumulate_lag_products

accumulate_lag_products

Add one day's high-pass residual to the running sums of lagged products, in place.

Description

u' and v' are pooled into the same sums. The sum of squares covers the whole padded tile, not only its interior, so each lag can be normalised by the variances at both its ends: normalising by the reference point alone gave correlations up to 27, since a correlation is bounded by 1 only with the symmetric form.

$$P_x(k) \mathrel{+}= u'_{i}\,u'_{i+k} + v'_{i}\,v'_{i+k},\qquad P_y(k) \text{ likewise in } j,\qquad P_0 \mathrel{+}= u'^2 + v'^2$$

Syntax

accumulate_lag_products(hu, hv, kmax, Px, Py, P0_pad)

Input Arguments

hu, hv — float
(1, jl+2kmax, il+2kmax) residual, with a kmax-wide margin
kmax — int
Largest lag, in grid points
Px, Py — float
(kmax, jl, il) running sums of lags 1 to kmax in x and y
P0_pad — float
(jl+2kmax, il+2kmax) running sum of u'^2 + v'^2

Output Arguments

None.

Example

th = 2*np.pi*t/nt5; h = np.cos(k6*(np.arange(nx6+2*km)-km)+th)[None, None]*np.ones((1, ny6+2*km, nx6+2*km)); Bl.accumulate_lag_products(h, 0*h, km, Px, Py, P0)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.pipelines.build_noise_lscale.accumulate_lag_products", "noisekit.pipelines.build_noise_lscale.efold_map"):
    km = 5; nt5 = 16; ny6, nx6 = 8, 64; k6 = 2*np.pi*4/nx6; Px, Py = np.zeros((km, ny6, nx6)), np.zeros((km, ny6, nx6)); P0 = np.zeros((ny6+2*km, nx6+2*km))
    for t in range(nt5):

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines.build_noise_lscale › efold_map

efold_map

The lag at which each point's correlation first drops below 1/e.

Description

Linear interpolation between the two lags around the crossing; lag 0 is 1. Where it never drops below 1/e within kmax, the length is at least kmax: it is returned as kmax and flagged as censored.

$$L = (k-1) + \frac{\rho_{k-1} - e^{-1}}{\rho_{k-1} - \rho_k},\qquad k = \min\{k : \rho_k < e^{-1}\}$$

Syntax

L, censored = efold_map(rho, kmax)

Input Arguments

rho — float
(kmax, jl, il) correlation at lags 1 to kmax
kmax — int
Largest lag

Output Arguments

L — float
(jl, il) e-folding lag, in grid points; exactly kmax where censored
censored — bool
(jl, il) True where rho never dropped below 1/e: the true length is at least kmax

Example

L0 = 5.5; Lm, cm = Bl.efold_map(np.exp(-np.arange(1, 21)/L0)[:, None, None]*np.ones((20, 2, 2)), 20); ok("e-fold", Lm - L0, 1.1/(8*L0)); yes("not censored", not cm.any())

    for t in range(nt5):
        th = 2*np.pi*t/nt5; h = np.cos(k6*(np.arange(nx6+2*km)-km)+th)[None, None]*np.ones((1, ny6+2*km, nx6+2*km)); Bl.accumulate_lag_products(h, 0*h, km, Px, Py, P0)
    ok("rho_x = cos(k l)", Px[:, 3, 10]/P0[3+km, 10+km] - np.cos(k6*np.arange(1, km+1)), 1e-6); ok("rho_y = 1", Py[:, 3, 10]/P0[3+km, 10+km] - 1, 1e-6)
    L0 = 5.5; Lm, cm = Bl.efold_map(np.exp(-np.arange(1, 21)/L0)[:, None, None]*np.ones((20, 2, 2)), 20); ok("e-fold", Lm - L0, 1.1/(8*L0)); yes("not censored", not cm.any())

main

Command-line entry point: measure the spatial correlation length of the GLORYS04 small-scale residual.

Description

The residual is the high-passed baroclinic velocity. Its lagged correlations in x and y over time give the e-folding lengths and their ratio, written as the length-scale input of the stochastic noise. Runs tiled under mpirun; its --sigma must match the one used for the noise amplitude.

$$\rho_x(k) = \frac{P_x(k)}{\sqrt{P_0(i)\,P_0(i+k)}},\qquad L_x = \text{efold}(\rho_x)\, e_{1t}$$

main()

None.

Output Arguments

None.

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines

pipelines.build_noise_sigma

MPI-tiled production script: read GLORYS04's barotropic-removed daily u/v (daily-baroclinic/, from build_baroclinic_daily.py), high-pass filter each day IN PLACE per rank (spatial tile + halo read straight off disk -- no MPI communication, see mpi_orca.read_slab_with_halo), fold the high-pass residual into a running (Welford) joint mean/variance/covariance, and at the end downsample the result onto the eORCA1 grid and write it as noise_sigma.nc -- the file tlu_gss.F90 already knows how to read (ln_tlu_stat / cn_tlu_stat_file), with EXACTLY the schema it expects: u_tavg, v_tavg, u_tvar, v_tvar, uv_tvcov, all (z, y, x) on the eORCA1 grid domain_cfg.nc describes.

Why a high-pass instead of the coarse-grain-then-subtract residual -------------------------------------------------------------------- build_noise_BcResid_stats.py computes the same *kind* of quantity (the sub-eORCA1-scale part of the flow) a different way: low-pass, bin-average onto eORCA1, reconstruct on the fine grid, subtract. That extra bin-average/reconstruct round trip mainly buys "the resolved part sits exactly on eORCA1's own discretisation" -- a small conceptual refinement, not different physics. A direct spatial high-pass (raw - low-pass, same sigma) removes the same band of scales more simply, is the same operation the SBC pipeline itself already uses elsewhere (see the noise-generation design notes sec 4.2.3's H operator), and -- the reason this script exists -- factorises cleanly into a per-tile, per-day, disk-halo-read operation with no inter-rank communication at all, unlike the coarse-grain step (which needs a global bin-average across tile boundaries). See the noise-generation design notes sec 3.1 for the shared design background.

Two halo modes -- read-from-disk (day loop) vs exchange (post-processing) --------------------------------------------------------------------------- Every rank owns one (nz, jl, il) horizontal tile, ALL 75 levels ("z-pencil", same shape as mpi_filter.py), for the ENTIRE 2-year day loop -- the tiling is decided once up front from the (static) grid size and never changes. Two DIFFERENT spatial filters run in this script, and they get their halo two different ways:

1. Per-day HIGH-PASS (day loop, `highpass_tile` / `process_one_day`).

Because the source files are read-only and every rank can open any one
of them independently, the halo this Gaussian filter needs is read
DIRECTLY OFF DISK (mpi_orca.read_slab_with_halo) instead of exchanged
with neighbouring ranks after reading just the interior. This removes
ALL per-day MPI traffic -- the day loop itself does zero communication.

2. Post-processing anti-alias LOW-PASS (`exchange_lowpass`, once, after

the day loop, before the eORCA1 downsample -- same purpose as
build_noise_stat.py's own pre-downsample low-pass). This filter's
input is the FINISHED Welford mean/variance/covariance -- a result
that lives only in this rank's memory, computed by folding 365+ days
together. There is no file to re-read a wider window from, so this
step genuinely needs a halo EXCHANGE with neighbouring ranks
(mpi_orca.add_halo / exchange_halo, the same primitives `mpi_filter.py`
uses) -- the one and only place this script does per-tile MPI
communication. Because it runs once (not once per day), the cost is
irrelevant next to the day loop's.

Besides that one exchange (and the trailing gathers below), the only other communication in the whole run is a handful of ONE-TIME gathers after the day loop, to assemble the finished (nz, ny_g, nx_g) statistics on rank 0 for the downsample + write.

Memory: O(1) in the number of days (Welford), same discipline as build_noise_BcResid_stats.py / build_noise_BcBtS_stats.py. Per rank, working set is a handful of (nz, jl+2hw, il+2hw) tiles plus the Welford aggregate of the same shape -- with, say, an 8x8 tiling (jl,il ~ 128, 180) and hw=32, that is a few hundred MB, not the several GB a single full-domain rank would need.

Run ---

# one-time correctness check (serial vs an 8x8 tiling vs the whole-domain
# reference smoother, one day only -- see check_tiling() below):
mpirun -np 64 .../python build_noise_sigma.py --check

# production: full 2-year archive, 8x8 = 64 ranks
mpirun -np 64 .../python build_noise_sigma.py

# production: one year only
mpirun -np 64 .../python build_noise_sigma.py --year 2015

# quick smoke test: a handful of days, any rank count (incl. serial)
python build_noise_sigma.py --limit 3

Choosing the tile count: any perfect square (mpi_orca.Decomp.from_comm's only requirement); pick P*P <= (free cores), and hw <= min(jl, il) is NOT required here (read_slab_with_halo has no neighbour to run out of, unlike add_halo) so a narrow tile with a wide halo is fine, just wasteful (a tile narrower than hw re-reads a lot of overlap). 8x8 = 64 ranks against a (1021, 1442) grid gives tiles ~ (128, 180) against hw = ceil(4*8) = 32 -- comfortable.

Runtime: high-pass filtering here is the SAME per-point cost as build_noise_BcResid_stats.py's smoothing step (~9 s/component/day full-domain, serial) -- but split across P*P tiles with no communication overhead per day, so wall time should drop roughly by that factor (64x tiling => minutes rather than hours for the full 2-year archive, network/ disk I/O rather than compute becomes the likely bottleneck at that point). Not yet benchmarked at full scale; the --check run measures one day first.

_masked_gaussian_padded

Land-aware Gaussian low-pass of an array that already carries its halo.

Description

The field times the mask and the mask are smoothed with the same kernel and divided, a weighted average over wet points; where the smoothed mask is below 0.01 the result is 0. orcakit.filters.lowpass with smooth=filters.gaussian does the same.

$$\tilde f = \frac{G_\sigma * (f m)}{G_\sigma * m} \text{ where } G_\sigma * m > 0.01,\ \text{else } 0$$

Syntax

low = _masked_gaussian_padded(a, w, sigma)

Input Arguments

a — float
(nz, jl+2hw, il+2hw) padded field
w — float
Same shape, wet mask
sigma — float
Gaussian lengthscale, in grid points; levels are not mixed

Output Arguments

low — float
Low-pass, same padded shape

Example

lp5 = Bs._masked_gaussian_padded(a, w, sig5); ok("low-pass transfer", rerr(lp5[:, 30:-30, hw5:-hw5], G5*a[:, 30:-30, hw5:-hw5]), 2e-3)
Whole test

    a = np.cos(k5*(np.arange(nx5+2*hw5)-hw5))[None, None]*np.ones((nz5, ny5+2*hw5, nx5+2*hw5)); w = np.ones_like(a)
    lp5 = Bs._masked_gaussian_padded(a, w, sig5); ok("low-pass transfer", rerr(lp5[:, 30:-30, hw5:-hw5], G5*a[:, 30:-30, hw5:-hw5]), 2e-3)
    hp5 = Bs.highpass_tile(a, w, sig5, hw5); yes("interior shape", hp5.shape == (nz5, ny5, nx5)); ok("high-pass transfer", rerr(hp5[:, 20:-20], (1-G5)*a[:, 20+hw5:-20-hw5, hw5:-hw5]), 2e-3)
    yes("margin kept", Bs.highpass_tile(a, w, sig5, hw5, margin=4).shape == (nz5, ny5+8, nx5+8))

highpass_tile

Land-aware Gaussian high-pass of a tile whose halo was read from disk.

Description

Pairs with mpi_orca.read_slab_with_halo, so there is no halo exchange. A margin of halo can be kept around the result, for lagged correlations with nearby points. orcakit.filters.highpass does the same on the whole grid.

$$f' = (f - \tilde f)\, m$$

hp = highpass_tile(a, w, sigma, hw)hp = highpass_tile(a, w, sigma, hw, margin=0)

sigma — float
Gaussian lengthscale, in grid points
hw — int
Halo width, at least ceil(4 sigma); the caller makes sure of it
margin — int — default 0
Halo cells kept around the result, at most hw; 0 for the bare interior. build_noise_lscale.py keeps kmax to correlate interior points with their neighbours without a second read

Output Arguments

(nz, jl+2margin, il+2margin) field minus low-pass, exactly 0 on land

exchange_lowpass

Anti-alias low-pass of a finished statistic, with its halo exchanged between ranks.

Description

A statistic summed over many days exists only in memory, so its halo comes from the neighbouring tiles rather than from disk. It is applied once, before the statistic is sampled onto a coarser grid.

$$\tilde s = \frac{G_\sigma * (s m)}{G_\sigma * m}\, m$$

Syntax

low = exchange_lowpass(dec, field, wet, sigma, is_meridional)low = exchange_lowpass(dec, field, wet, sigma, is_meridional, point='T')

check_tiling

Check both halo modes on one day against whole-domain references.

Description

The tiled high-pass, with the halo read from disk, is compared with reference_highpass; that result, low-passed with the halo exchanged, is compared with reference_lowpass. One day stands in for a statistic: this checks the code, not any physical number.

$$\max |f_{\text{tiled}} - f_{\text{ref}}|,\quad \text{rms}(f_{\text{tiled}} - f_{\text{ref}})$$

This run's decomposition, serial or tiled
uf, vf — str
One day's files
sigma — float
High-pass lengthscale, in grid points
hw — int
Halo width
sigma_lp — float
Anti-alias low-pass lengthscale, in grid points

None.

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines

pipelines.runvar_dmd

D1 and D2: time-varying noise amplitude from DMD of a running variance.

Smooths velocity, takes its variance (or standard deviation) over a sliding window of snapshots, decomposes the anomalies with exact or kernel DMD, keeps one mode per conjugate pair, samples onto eORCA1 and writes noise_DMDstatistics.nc for tlu_gss.F90.

Ported from the earlier CMEMS running-variance and kernel DMD notebooks. Differences from the notebooks: - no grid flip, and the whole grid is read, not the [-2::-1, 1:-1] crop; - snapshots stay in time order. The notebooks start with i = -whs, which

stores the first window in the last column;

- the tapers are computed here, not read from CMECS_to_eOrca1.nc; - the default statistic is variance, as in the backup notebook, which

produced CMECS_varDMD_2016-2017.nc. The later notebook switched to std.

python -m noisekit.pipelines.runvar_dmd --out noise_DMDstatistics.nc --start 2016-01 --end 2016-12

Functions

_months_beforeThe month n months before a given one.
window_statRunning variance or standard deviation of a smoothed, tapered velocity.
window_stat.snapshotsThe cleaned, smoothed and tapered snapshots, one at a time.
decomposeExact or kernel DMD of a matrix of anomalies.
runD1 and D2: modes of the running variance of u and v, as NEMO's noise input.
run.coarseTaper, sample onto eORCA1 and taper again.
mainCommand-line entry point of D1 and D2.

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines.runvar_dmd › window_stat

window_stat

Running variance or standard deviation of a smoothed, tapered velocity.

Description

How strongly a field varies itself changes in time, with the seasons for example. Each window's statistic follows that change. The record starts window - 1 months before start, so the first window ends at start.

$$s_t = \mathrm{var}\big(\tau\, G_\sigma * u\big) \text{ over } t - W + 1, \dots, t$$

Syntax

stat = window_stat(data, var, start, end, window, sigma, taper)stat = window_stat(data, var, start, end, window, sigma, taper, stat='var', level=None)

Input Arguments

data — module
datakit module, e.g. datakit.cmems
var — str
'vozocrtx' or 'vomecrty'
start — str
Month of the first window's end
end — str
Month of the last window's end
window — int
Snapshots per window
sigma — float
Gaussian smoothing of each snapshot, in grid points; 0 for none
taper — float
Coastal taper the snapshots are multiplied by
stat — str — default 'var'
'var' or 'std'
level — int — default None
One level, or None for all

Output Arguments

stat — float — default 'var'
(nt, [nz,] ny, nx), one per window

Example

s = Rv.window_stat(fr, "vozocrtx", "2000-03", "2000-08", 3, 0, np.ones((20, 30)), "var", 0); yes("window count", s.shape[0] == 6); ok("var = 2/3", s - 2/3, 1e-12)
s = Rv.window_stat(fr, "vozocrtx", "2000-03", "2000-08", 3, 0, np.ones((20, 30)), "std", 0); ok("std", s - np.sqrt(2/3), 1e-12)
Whole test

with test("noisekit.pipelines.runvar_dmd.decompose"):
    ka = np.arange(2, 40); xv = vmean + vamp*np.cos(2*om*(ka-1)); direct = np.array([np.var(a_*np.cos(om*np.arange(k-2, k+1))) for k in ka])
    ok("closed form of the running variance", xv - direct, 1e-12)

    mds, eig, ct = Rv.decompose(Xa, 2, None, 5.); ok("exact DMD finds exp(2 i omega)", match(np.exp([2j*om, -2j*om]), eig), 1e-10); ok("continuous", match(np.array([2j*om, -2j*om])/5., ct), 1e-10)

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines.runvar_dmd › run

run

D1 and D2: modes of the running variance of u and v, as NEMO's noise input.

Description

The running variance follows how variability changes in time. Its DMD gives a few oscillating spatial patterns; one mode per conjugate pair is kept, and the mean and modes are tapered at the coasts, sampled onto eORCA1 and written in the format of tlu_gss.F90. D1 uses exact DMD, D2 kernel DMD.

$$s(t) \approx \bar s + \mathrm{Re}\sum_k 2\, b_k \phi_k\, e^{\lambda^c_k t}$$

Syntax

run(out, start, end)run(out, start, end, dataset='cmems', window=3, rank=100.0, kernel=None, sigma=4, map_file=None, domain=DOMAIN_ORCA1, nmodes=None, stat='var', level=None)

Input Arguments

out — str
File to write
start — str
Month of the first window's end
end — str
Month of the last window's end
dataset — str — default 'cmems'
datakit module name
window — int — default 3
Snapshots per window
rank — float — default 100.0
Rank, or share of information to keep
kernel — str — default None
None for D1, 'linear' or 'poly' for D2
sigma — float — default 4
Gaussian smoothing of each snapshot, in grid points
map_file — str — default None
Index map cache, default <out dir>/<dataset>_to_eorca1.nc
domain — str — default DOMAIN_ORCA1
eORCA1 domain_cfg
nmodes — int — default None
Keep this many modes with the largest energy, or None for all
stat — str — default 'var'
'var' or 'std'
level — int — default None
One level, or None for all

Output Arguments

None.

Example

Rv.run(out, "2000-03", "2000-47", "faker2", window=3, rank=2, sigma=0, map_file=os.path.join(TMP, "rmap.nc"), domain=dom2)
Whole test
with test("noisekit.pipelines.runvar_dmd.run"):
    def g_r(v, k):
        # the phase varies with x, so the running variance has rank 2
        return a_*np.cos(om*k + 2*np.pi*np.arange(60)/60)[None, None]*np.ones((3, 40, 60), dtype=np.float64)
    fr2 = fake("faker2", g_r, ny=40, nx=60, tmask=np.ones((3, 40, 60))); fr2.nsnap = 47
    dom2 = domain("dom2.nc")
    out = os.path.join(TMP, "rv.nc")
    Rv.run(out, "2000-03", "2000-47", "faker2", window=3, rank=2, sigma=0, map_file=os.path.join(TMP, "rmap.nc"), domain=dom2)
    with netCDF4.Dataset(out) as nc:
        um = nc["uavg"][:]; print("   modes", nc["omega"].shape, "omega", nc["omega"][:])
        ok("mean running variance", rerr(um[0, 8, 10], vmean), 1e-6); ok("written omega x dt", (match(np.array([2*om/Rv.DT_MONTH]), np.abs(nc["omega"][:])))*Rv.DT_MONTH, 1e-6)

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines

pipelines.v4_bcbts

V4: barotropic/baroclinic split noise statistics from daily GLORYS04.

Keeps running statistics of the barotropic and baroclinic parts of u and v, low-passes them, samples them onto the eORCA1 grid and writes them. to_tlu() converts the result to the file tlu_gss.F90 reads.

Ported from the earlier scripts build_noise_BcBtS_stats.py and build_TLUstat_from_BcBtS.py.

python -m noisekit.pipelines.v4_bcbts --out stats.nc --tlu tlu_stats.nc

Functions

lowpassMask-aware low-pass of the statistics.

to_orca1Sample fields onto eORCA1 at the nearest GLORYS04 point.
to_tluWrite NEMO's noise statistics file from the V4 statistics, baroclinic part only.

to_tlu

Write NEMO's noise statistics file from the V4 statistics, baroclinic part only.

Description

The file has u_tavg, v_tavg, u_tvar, v_tvar and uv_tvcov. uv_tvcov is 0: it is not computed here, and tlu_gss.F90 does not use it.

$$(u, v)_{tavg} = \mu_{bc},\quad (u, v)_{tvar} = \sigma^2_{bc},\quad uv_{tvcov} = 0$$

to_tlu(stats_file, tlu_file)

stats_file — str
Statistics written by main
tlu_file — str
File to write

None.

py-kits › noisekit › pipelines

pipelines.variance

V1, V2, V3: constant-variance noise statistics.

Optionally smooths each snapshot, keeps running mean, variance and covariance of u and v, optionally low-passes them, samples them onto eORCA1 and writes them.

V3 (GLORYS04 surface):  --dataset glorys04 --level 0 --lowpass 12 --names noise_stat
V2 (filtered CMEMS):    --dataset cmems --smooth 4
V1 (CMEMS):             --dataset cmems

--names picks the variable names: 'tlu' (u_tavg, ... as tlu_gss.F90 reads) or 'noise_stat' (umean, ... as build_noise_stat.py wrote).

The flux variant of V2 (download_and_process.py) is not covered.

Functions

runV1 to V3: mean, variance and covariance of u and v, sampled onto eORCA1.
run.smootherThe ORCA Gaussian for one point and fold sign.
mainCommand-line entry point of V1 to V3.
py-kits › noisekit › pipelines.variance › run

run

V1 to V3: mean, variance and covariance of u and v, sampled onto eORCA1.

Description

Snapshots may be smoothed first and the statistics low-passed after. The covariance pairs U(i,j) with V(i,j), the points of the same index, as NEMO's noise input expects.

$$\mu,\ \sigma^2_u,\ \sigma^2_v,\ c_{uv} \text{ of } G_{\sigma_1} * u,\ G_{\sigma_1} * v,\ \text{then } \text{masked\_smooth}_{\sigma_2}$$

pipelines.w_modes

W1: vertical-velocity modes by DMD, for tlu_gss.F90 (CMECS_wmodes.nc).

Computes w by integrating the horizontal divergence upward from the bottom, decomposes it with exact DMD, keeps the modes near the unit circle and samples them onto eORCA1.

Ported from the earlier CMEMS w-noise notebook. This deliberately differs from that notebook, so CMECS_wmodes.nc cannot be reproduced with it: - the notebook differenced v[1:] - v[:-1] on a flipped grid, which gives the

snapshot_w

W from one pair of 3D velocities, without partial steps.

Description

Uses the 1D reference thicknesses and a divergence without thicknesses, so near the sea floor it differs from orcakit.grid_c.vertical_velocity.

run

W1: DMD modes of the vertical velocity, as NEMO's noise input.

Description

w is computed from u and v, decomposed by exact DMD, and the modes near the unit circle are sampled onto eORCA1 and written in the format of tlu_gss.F90.

$$w(t) \approx \bar w + \mathrm{Re}\sum_{|\,|\lambda_k| - 1| \le \text{tol}} b_k \phi_k\, \lambda_k^{\,t}$$

File to write

end — str
Last date

datakit module name
rank — float — default 100.0
Rank, or share of information to keep
tol — float — default 0.01
Largest distance of |eig| from 1 kept

Index map cache, default <out dir>/<dataset>_to_eorca1.nc

eORCA1 domain_cfg

Example

Whole test
with test("noisekit.pipelines.w_modes.run"):
    mt = wgrid(); nzw = 4; jj, ii = np.mgrid[:nyw, :nxw].astype(float)
    kx_, ky_ = 2*np.pi*3/(nxw*dxw), 2*np.pi*2/(nyw*dyw); pw_ = 2*np.pi/9
    def g_w(v, k):
        # uniform divergence plus two oscillating patterns in quadrature
        return np.stack([1e-6*(ii+.5)*dxw + .5e-6*np.cos(pw_*k)*np.sin(kx_*(ii+.5)*dxw)/kx_ if v == "vozocrtx" else 2e-6*(jj+.5)*dyw + .5e-6*np.sin(pw_*k)*np.sin(ky_*(jj+.5)*dyw)/ky_]*nzw)
    fw = fake("fakew", g_w, ny=nyw, nx=nxw, e1t=mt["e1t"], e2t=mt["e2t"], e1v=mt["e1v"], e2u=mt["e2u"], e3t_0=10*np.ones(nzw), tmask=mt["tmask"]); fw.nsnap = 36
    dom3 = domain("dom3.nc", ny=10, nx=12, nz=nzw); out = os.path.join(TMP, "wm.nc")
    Wm.run(out, "2000-01", "2000-36", "fakew", rank=2, tol=.05, map_file=os.path.join(TMP, "wmap.nc"), domain=dom3)
    with netCDF4.Dataset(out) as nc:
        ok("mean w at the surface = -(1e-6+2e-6) e3 n_wet", rerr(nc["wavg"][0, 5, 6], -3e-6*10*3), 2e-2); yes("modes written", nc["omega"].size > 0)
        print("   omega x dt / (2 pi / 9) =", np.abs(nc["omega"][:])*Wm.DT_MONTH/(2*np.pi/9))
        ok("mode frequency", match(np.array([2*np.pi/9/Wm.DT_MONTH]), np.abs(nc["omega"][:]))*Wm.DT_MONTH, 1e-6)

py-kits

modredkit

Model reduction: the decompositions that turn a long record of fields into a few patterns.

A record of ocean fields is huge, but most of its variability lives in a few spatial patterns. Proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) finds the patterns that carry the most variance; dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) finds patterns that each oscillate at one frequency and grow or decay at one rate, and its kernel form extends it to nonlinear dynamics. These modes are used to build reduced models and, in this library, to give the stochastic noise a structure in space and time.

Conventions: snapshot matrices are (space, time), one snapshot per column, and the decompositions work in float64. A rank given as an int is a number of modes; as a float it is a share of information to keep (100.0 keeps all).

Modules

podsnapshot POD, weighted or not, for one field or several fields together
dmdexact DMD, kernel DMD, windowed multi-level DMD, amplitudes, eigenvalue filters and plots
modesworking with snapshot matrices and modes: packing fields, selecting modes, rebuilding records
py-kits › modredkit

dmd

Dynamic mode decomposition: exact, kernel and windowed multi-level DMD, with amplitudes, eigenvalue filters, reshaping helpers and plots.

Written by F.L. Tucciarone, 2023. Taken from the classDMD module of the earlier model-reduction code (2026-09-06) and renamed dmd.py -- it is a module of functions, not a class.

getConjugatePairsMask, RemGtT, CleanUnitCircle, PlotCircle, PlotAmplitudes.

The classes ``DMD_vecmodes`` and ``DMD_phyModes`` were broken and unused, and are gone; they are not in this repository.

py-kits › modredkit › dmd › RelativeInformationContent

RelativeInformationContent

The rank that keeps a given share of the singular values.

Description

Truncating a decomposition keeps the dominant structures and drops noise; the question is where to cut. This picks the rank whose singular values add up to a given share of their total, or takes a rank given directly.

The share uses the singular values S, not S^2, so it is not the share of variance; rank_from_energy in pod uses S^2.

$$r = \min\Big\{ r : \frac{\sum_{k \le r} S_k}{\sum_k S_k} \gtrsim \tau \Big\}$$

Syntax

r = RelativeInformationContent(S)r = RelativeInformationContent(S, r=None, verbose=False)

Input Arguments

S — float
Singular values, in decreasing order
r — int/float — default None
An int is a rank, capped at len(S); a float is the share to keep, as a fraction, or as a percentage if above 1; None keeps all
verbose — bool — default False
Plot the cumulative share and the rank chosen

Output Arguments

r — int — default None
Rank

Example

S_ = np.array([4., 3., 2., 1.]); ok("float fraction", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_, .7) - 2, 0); ok("float percent", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_, 90.) - 3, 0)
ok("int means that rank", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_, 2) - 2, 0); ok("None keeps all", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_) - 4, 0)
Whole test
with test("modredkit.dmd.RelativeInformationContent"):
    S_ = np.array([4., 3., 2., 1.]); ok("float fraction", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_, .7) - 2, 0); ok("float percent", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_, 90.) - 3, 0)
    ok("int means that rank", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_, 2) - 2, 0); ok("None keeps all", D.RelativeInformationContent(S_) - 4, 0)

SVD

Thin singular value decomposition of a snapshot matrix, truncated to a rank.

Description

The SVD gives the orthogonal structures that best represent the snapshots, ordered by importance; it is the first step of DMD and of POD.

$$X \approx U_r\, \mathrm{diag}(S_r)\, V_r^{*}$$

Syntax

U, S, Vh = SVD(X, r)U, S, Vh = SVD(X, r, verbose=False)

Input Arguments

X — float
(n, m) matrix of snapshots, one per column
r — int/float
Rank, or share of information to keep (see RelativeInformationContent); None keeps all
verbose — bool — default False
Print the shapes

Output Arguments

U — float
(n, r) left singular vectors
S — float
(r,) singular values
Vh — float
(r, m) right singular vectors, conjugate-transposed

Example

Xr = np.random.default_rng(3).standard_normal((30, 12)); U, S, Vh = D.SVD(Xr, None); ok("full", U*S@Vh - Xr, 1e-12)

ok("float 100.0 keeps all", D.SVD(Xr, 100.0)[1].size - 12, 0)
Whole test
